Scientists Uncover Why a Common Nutrient Can Be Dangerous for Blood Vessels

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (809 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New research suggests that dietary phosphate may influence blood vessel damage and lifespan, with crucial implications for people with chronic kidney disease.
  • According to recent reports, A newly identified role for a protein in the kidneys could help explain why excess phosphate in the blood contributes to hardened arteries and shorter lifespans.
  • The study, published in October 2026, identified TMEM174 as an important regulator of blood phosphate levels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New research suggests that dietary phosphate may influence blood vessel damage and lifespan, with crucial implications for people with chronic kidney disease.

According to recent reports, A newly identified role for a protein in the kidneys could help explain why excess phosphate in the blood contributes to hardened arteries and shorter lifespans. Researchers at the University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine found that animals lacking this protein developed more calcium deposits in their blood vessels and died earlier, particularly when consuming a diet high in phosphate.

The study, published in October 2026, identified TMEM174 as an important regulator of blood phosphate levels. Reducing dietary phosphate lessened some of the harmful effects in animals deficient in the protein. The findings point to a potential treatment target for chronic kidney disease (CKD), a condition that makes it difficult for the body to eliminate excess phosphate.

The kidneys continuously filter phosphate from the bloodstream, removing excess amounts through urine while retaining enough to support essential functions such as bone formation. A protein called NPT2A helps maintain this balance by reabsorbing approximately three-quarters of the filtered phosphate and returning it to the blood.

In a recent development, the researchers discovered that TMEM174 acts as a counterbalance to NPT2A. By binding to NPT2A and reducing its activity, TMEM174 helps prevent excessive phosphate reabsorption. In animal models lacking TMEM174, phosphate regulation became disrupted, vascular calcification increased, and lifespan was significantly reduced.

Recent findings suggest that “We don’t fully understand how yet, but somehow TMEM174 is destabilizing NPT2A,” states Makoto Miyazaki, PhD, a research professor in the Division of Renal Diseases and Hypertension and senior author of the study. “And without enough TMEM174, homeostasis is disrupted.”.

According to recent reports, phosphorus is an essential nutrient found in meat, fish, dairy products, nuts, legumes, and whole grains. It is also commonly added to processed foods and beverages to improve flavor and extend shelf life. Unlike many naturally occurring phosphorus compounds, phosphate additives are generally absorbed more efficiently by the digestive system.

It has been revealed that although the body needs phosphorus, persistently elevated blood phosphate (hyperphosphatemia) can damage the cardiovascular system. Excess phosphate can cause smooth muscle cells in blood vessel walls to develop characteristics of bone-forming cells. These altered cells promote the accumulation of calcium phosphate crystals, causing blood vessels to stiffen (or calcify).

It has been revealed that healthy arteries expand and contract in response to changing blood flow. Calcification reduces that flexibility, contributing to vascular aging and increasing cardiovascular risks. In the newly introduced study, the combination of TMEM174 deficiency and a phosphate-rich diet accelerated this process in animals.

“Phosphate is really underestimated in terms of longevity in all mammals. The higher the concentration of phosphate in the blood, the shorter the lifespan,” says Miyazaki.

Sources indicate that elevated blood phosphate is relatively uncommon in the general population because healthy kidneys can usually remove the excess. In people with CKD, however, declining kidney function reduces phosphate excretion, allowing the mineral to accumulate in the bloodstream.

Recent findings suggest that this impaired phosphate regulation can contribute to vascular calcification, which is particularly common in people with kidney disease. The newly discovered role of TMEM174 suggests another potential source of vulnerability. Although TMEM174 deficiency appears to be primarily genetic rather than caused by CKD, researchers suspect that people affected by both conditions could face additional cardiovascular risks.

The experiments established a connection between TMEM174 deficiency, abnormal phosphate regulation, vascular calcification, and reduced survival in animal models. Whether differences in TMEM174 activity have comparable effects on cardiovascular health or lifespan in humans remains to be determined.

The findings suggest that treatments affecting TMEM174 or its interaction with NPT2A might help the kidneys eliminate more phosphate instead of returning it to the bloodstream. Such an approach could eventually provide another way to manage phosphate levels in people with CKD.

Dietary changes may also help. The researchers found that reducing phosphate intake partially protected animals lacking TMEM174 from harmful effects. Miyazaki notes that limiting phosphate-rich processed foods, including fast food, deli meats, and sodas, could be beneficial. However, phosphate occurs naturally in so many foods that dietary restrictions alone may be insufficient, particularly for people with impaired kidney function.

Future research will examine how TMEM174 interacts with other proteins and hormones involved in phosphate regulation. Miyazaki also hopes to investigate why calcium deposits are so prevalent in the blood vessels of people with CKD.

“Scientists have been studying phosphate homeostasis for over 100 years, so to still find a new protein that regulates phosphate is kind of unique,” says Miyazaki.

Industry observers note that reference: “TMEM174 deficiency reduces longevity by promoting phosphate-driven vascular calcification” by Jose G. Miranda, Judith Blaine and Makoto Miyazaki, 2 October 2026, Scientific Reports. DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-74353-2.

  • The move clears the way for Senate Ethics Chairman James Lankford, R-Okla., to use his seniority to ascend to ranking Republican on the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which Paul currently chairs, and touches off several other shifts at the top of other committees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., leaves the Senate Republicans’ lunch in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., announced Wednesday he prepares to serve as the top Republican on the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee when Democrats take control of Congress next year.

The move clears the way for Senate Ethics Chairman James Lankford, R-Okla., to use his seniority to ascend to ranking Republican on the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which Paul currently chairs, and touches off several other shifts at the top of other committees.

Industry observers note that the move fit in with Sen. Lisa Murkowski’s bid to use her seniority to succeed Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, as top Republican on the Appropriations panel. If Paul did not go to the top spot on HELP, Murkowski, R-Alaska, would be next in line for that committee in the next Congress.

According to recent reports, murkowski is second in seniority on Appropriations to Collins, who was defeated for reelection. But she faces a potential challenge from Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., who is next in line behind her.

Paul remarked in a press release that he prepares to bring the same approach to the HELP Committee as he did as chairman of Homeland, where he said he “challenged entrenched bureaucracies, forced federal officials to answer for their actions, and pulled back the curtain on what Washington tried to keep hidden.”.

Recent findings suggest that he cited calling Dr. Anthony Fauci before the committee to probe the former federal health official’s role in pandemic-related shutdowns and the origin of the COVID-19 virus, and releasing thousands of pages of pandemic-related documents. The panel voted in August to hold Fauci in criminal contempt of Congress for declining to answer questions about the pandemic during a highly charged hearing.

Related: Fauci could face criminal contempt charge following panel vote.

Paul, an ophthalmologist, said at HELP he will “stand against efforts to put Washington between Americans and their doctors, their children’s schools, and their paychecks.” He predicted “a rush toward socialism unlike anything we have seen” when the Democrat-controlled Congress convenes in January.

Lankford, in a separate statement, confirmed his interest in becoming the ranking member of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. In many areas, he remarked, the panel can work in a bipartisan manner, and over the past decade he “worked across the aisle to improve emergency communications in federal buildings, strengthen the United States Postal Service, increase federal cybersecurity preparedness, government transparency, and the use of artificial intelligence.”.

But he added that his job also would be to “push back on a [Democratic] majority that goes too far . . . Oversight is responsible, but obstruction is unacceptable.”.

Recent findings suggest that lankford said he would work together with the likely committee chair, Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., “when we can agree and be a fierce opposition if there is an attempt to undercut our nation’s security.”.

#42925. A Common Heart Failure Warning Sign May Actually Be Causing Dangerous Blood Clots

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1004 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Scitechdaily ↗ Open Full Page

A Common Heart Failure Warning Sign May Actually Be Causing Dangerous Blood Clots

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1004 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A hormone used to detect heart trouble can also promote dangerous blood clots in experiments, pointing scientists toward a possible way to prevent blockages without disrupting normal healing.
  • Industry observers note that heart disease remains the leading cause of death in the United States, claiming a life nearly every 34 seconds.
  • Sources indicate that the substance is a hormone called B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A hormone used to detect heart trouble can also promote dangerous blood clots in experiments, pointing scientists toward a possible way to prevent blockages without disrupting normal healing.

Industry observers note that heart disease remains the leading cause of death in the United States, claiming a life nearly every 34 seconds. For people living with heart failure, a condition in which the heart struggles to pump enough blood throughout the body, doctors often rely on blood tests to detect signs of cardiac stress. Now, researchers have discovered that one of these familiar warning signals may also contribute to a dangerous complication: blood clots that can block circulation and trigger life-threatening events.

Sources indicate that the substance is a hormone called B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP). Doctors routinely measure BNP and related protein fragments because elevated levels can indicate heart failure or other cardiovascular problems. Until now, BNP has largely been viewed as a marker of an overworked heart rather than a potential contributor to disease.

Researchers at the Texas A&M University Irma Lerma Rangel College of Pharmacy, part of Texas A&M Health, have found that elevated BNP can directly activate blood platelets and accelerate clot formation. The study, published in Blood, identifies a molecular pathway that could eventually offer a more targeted way to prevent dangerous blood clots.

According to recent reports, “We thought that BNP might not only act as a passive marker but actively contributes to the pathogenesis and progression of cardiovascular disease,” said Dr. Zhenyu Li, a professor of pharmaceutical sciences who led the research.

Industry observers note that platelets normally protect the body from blood loss. When a blood vessel is damaged, these tiny blood components gather at the injury and stick together to help stop bleeding. Problems arise when platelets become overly active and form clots inside blood vessels where they are not needed. Those clots can obstruct circulation, depriving tissues and organs of oxygen, and contribute to emergencies such as heart attacks and pulmonary embolisms, which occur when a clot blocks blood flow in the lungs.

Li’s team traced BNP’s effects to a receptor on the surface of platelets called natriuretic peptide receptor-A (NPRA). Receptors allow cells to respond to specific chemical signals, and the researchers found that BNP activates platelets by binding directly to NPRA.

Sources indicate that “It was previously unknown whether platelets even expressed this receptor,” Li explained. “We are the first team to investigate whether BNP directly activates platelets through the NPRA receptor.”.

Once BNP attaches to NPRA, it increases the amount of a signaling molecule called cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) inside platelets. This sets off a chain of cellular responses that makes platelets more likely to stick together and promotes clot growth. In experimental studies involving blood-vessel injury and pulmonary embolism, elevated BNP markedly accelerated clot formation.

Industry observers note that the researchers also examined what happened when NPRA was blocked or its gene was removed. Under those conditions, BNP could no longer increase cGMP levels or activate platelets, and the experiments showed protection against abnormal clotting.

“Knocking out the NPRA gene protected against these complications, proving the clotting process is mediated by the NPRA receptor,” Li noted.

Blood samples from patients with heart rhythm disorders provided additional evidence. In these patients, higher circulating BNP levels were associated with greater platelet activity. The finding supports a possible connection between BNP and clotting risk in humans, although the association alone does not establish that BNP directly causes blood clots in patients.

People with elevated BNP are already known to face a higher risk of serious cardiovascular events, including heart attacks and pulmonary embolisms. The newly identified pathway offers a possible biological explanation for that relationship. Li emphasized that the discovery emerged from years of work examining platelet activity and cardiovascular disease.

“It has been an ongoing, gradual progression—not a sudden breakthrough, but a logical continuation of our research over the past two decades,” he said.

The findings could have implications for how dangerous blood clots are prevented. Existing antiplatelet medications reduce the ability of platelets to form clots, but their effects throughout the body can increase the risk of serious internal bleeding. By targeting the interaction between BNP and NPRA, researchers hope to develop treatments that interfere with harmful clot formation while preserving the normal clotting needed to heal injuries.

Recent findings suggest that such treatments remain experimental. Li suggested that, in the meantime, physicians may need to monitor patients with elevated BNP more closely and consider whether antiplatelet therapy could help reduce their risk of clot-related complications.

Sources indicate that several questions also remain about the mechanism. Although platelets appear central to BNP-driven clotting, the researchers still need to establish how much of the effect comes specifically from NPRA receptors on platelets rather than receptors on other cells. Future studies will selectively remove NPRA from different cell types to clarify their respective roles.

“Platelets appear to be major contributors, and to confirm this further, we need to develop tissue-specific models,” Li remarked.

Recent findings suggest that the team is now working with Dr. Wenshe Liu, Regents Professor and Harry E. Bovay, Jr. Chair in Chemistry at the Texas A&M College of Arts and Sciences, to identify small molecules capable of blocking the BNP-NPRA interaction. Promising compounds will undergo further testing to determine whether they can prevent BNP-induced platelet activation and thrombosis without broadly disrupting healthy clotting.

“Because patients with high BNP levels face the greatest risk, targeting this pathway opens new opportunities to reduce thrombotic complications while minimizing standard side effects like severe bleeding,” Li said.

Reference: “BNP Promotes Platelet Activation and Thrombosis via its Receptor NPRA: A Paradigm Shift from Biomarker to Effector” by Yan Zhang, Guoying Zhang, Jiaqian Qi, Shahnaz Qadri, Sahebsadat Hajimirzaei, Zhuodong Chai, Yuqi Zhou, Ling Yang, Fatima Z Alshbool, Yihan Wei, Fadi T Khasawneh and Zhenyu Li, 22 September 2026, Blood. DOI: 10.1182/blood.2026025455.

Funding: NIH/National Institutes of Health, American Heart Association.

#42923. Scientists Discover That One Simple Desk Change Could Boost Productivity by Nearly $9,000 a Year

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1266 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Scitechdaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists Discover That One Simple Desk Change Could Boost Productivity by Nearly $9,000 a Year

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1266 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The desk you work at may have more influence on productivity than you think, with research involving over 10,000 employees linking standing desks to greater daily computer activity.
  • Sources indicate that for anyone who spends most of the workday in front of a computer, sitting for hours can leave the back aching, the neck stiff, and energy running low by midafternoon.
  • Now, a large study from Texas A&M University suggests that sit-stand desks may offer another advantage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The desk you work at may have more influence on productivity than you think, with research involving over 10,000 employees linking standing desks to greater daily computer activity.

Sources indicate that for anyone who spends most of the workday in front of a computer, sitting for hours can leave the back aching, the neck stiff, and energy running low by midafternoon. Standing up and moving around can help break up that routine, which is part of the appeal of height-adjustable desks. These workstations let employees switch between sitting and standing without stepping away from their work, offering a simple way to reduce physical strain and spend less time in one position.

Now, a large study from Texas A&M University suggests that sit-stand desks may offer another advantage. Employees using them averaged about 43 more minutes of active computer use each day than those working at traditional desks. Over a year, that difference could represent nearly $9,000 in potential productivity value per employee.

The research, published in Theoretical and Applied Ergonomics, was co-led by Dr. Mark Benden, a professor at Texas A&M’s School of Public Health, and Dr. Tricia Salzar, Regional Ergonomist for the U.S. Army Public Health Command Region, West.

Rather than relying on a small laboratory experiment, the researchers examined how people used their computers during ordinary workdays. “We analyzed a huge dataset of more than 10,000 workers over a yearlong period, comparing the total computer use of traditional desk users and height-adjustable desk users,” Benden noted.

Industry observers note that the team combined employee comfort surveys with software measurements of computer activity, including keystrokes, words typed, mouse clicks, and typing errors. This allowed the researchers to examine both how workers felt about their workstations and how actively they used their computers.

“It was important that we collected subjective measurements, like employee survey responses of their comfort and objective measurements of computer activity through software, to analyze how people engaged with their work,” Benden remarked.

In a recent development, employees with sit-stand desks averaged 3.66 hours of active computer time per day, compared with 2.95 hours among those using conventional desks. That difference of approximately 43 minutes may seem modest during a single workday, but the researchers calculated that it amounted to roughly 171 additional hours annually, equivalent to more than four 40-hour workweeks.

The difference also extended beyond time spent using a computer. Employees with adjustable desks generally typed more words and recorded more keystrokes, suggesting that the additional activity was accompanied by greater measurable output.

“The data showed that people aren’t just engaging with their work, they are producing output in a meaningful way,” Benden said.

In a recent development, using a standardized hourly wage of approximately $52, the researchers calculated that those 171 additional hours could represent nearly $9,000 in annual productivity value for each employee. The figure is an estimate based on computer activity and hourly wages, rather than a demonstrated increase in firm profits or a financial return that accounts for the cost of purchasing the desks.

“Our findings were exciting because they suggest that height-adjustable desks can directly influence overall work output and economic organizational productivity,” Benden remarked.

Recent findings suggest that the results are encouraging, although the comparison does not establish that the desks themselves caused the difference in activity. The measurements also do not directly show whether employees experienced less back pain, reduced fatigue, or better concentration. Those remain potential benefits rather than outcomes established by the reported computer-use findings.

It has been revealed that still, the results add to a broader discussion about how the spaces people work in can influence their daily experience. Employers often look to new software, training, and management strategies to improve performance, while the physical surroundings receive less attention.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s what we call the ‘workplace effect,’” Benden said. “The direct impact that the physical work environment has on the behavior, health, psychological well-being, and even engagement and performance of employees.”.

A sit-stand desk is a relatively straightforward example of that idea. Instead of requiring someone to remain seated throughout the day, it allows them to adjust their position as their comfort and tasks change. For workers who spend much of their time at a computer, that flexibility may make long workdays more manageable.

According to recent reports, “It can have a profound effect,” Benden remarked. “Alternating between different working positions promotes better health outcomes by reducing physical strain and encouraging movement for those who might otherwise spend most of their workday sedentary.”.

The possibility of easing physical discomfort while supporting more sustained energy and longer periods of focused work makes adjustable desks appealing to employees. For employers, the potential benefit is a workforce that can remain productive while working in a more comfortable environment.

“It has a cumulative, positive effect for both employers and employees,” Benden said.

Benden believes these findings demonstrate why workplace design deserves a larger role in conversations about employee health and organizational performance.

“The design of the workplace itself can be a powerful driver of human health and performance, including better engagement, productivity, and organizational success,” Benden noted.

“The implications are hard to ignore,” Benden stated. “When we design workplaces around employees and their needs, better health, better performance, and better organizational outcomes follow.”.

In a recent development, understanding that relationship has been a major focus of Benden’s career. A former Army Reserve officer, engineer, healthcare professional, inventor, and internationally recognized researcher, he has spent decades investigating how work environments affect the people who use them.

“We spend a lot of time at work,” Benden said. “It’s my passion to make sure that workers feel supported in their workplace, built on informed and guided scientific evidence.”.

He currently directs the Center for Worker Health at Texas A&M, which brings together engineering, management, and technology through interdisciplinary research, innovation, and education. Its work focuses on developing practical improvements in worker health and efficiency, while helping students turn their ideas into real-world applications.

“The Center partners with industry nationwide, to develop innovative, impactful systems and practices that have a direct effect on worker health and efficiency,” Benden said. “We also train students and give them the platform to be as creative as possible to turn new ideas into impactful applications.”.

It has been revealed that the research is also expanding beyond furniture and ergonomics. As artificial intelligence becomes a more common part of office work, Benden is interested in how these technologies might interact with the physical environments in which employees perform their jobs.

“Artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly integrated into daily work,” Benden stated. “Just as we’ve studied how the physical environment affects human health and performance, we’re interested in understanding how emerging AI technologies could influence the physical workspace and outcomes of organizations.”.

For organizations considering changes to their offices, the findings suggest that improving the everyday experience of working at a computer may be worth examining alongside investments in new technology. Whether the goal is to reduce physical strain, encourage movement, or support productivity, even something as familiar as a desk could have a role to play.

“The next breakthrough may not come from working harder, but from designing workspaces and systems that help people work smarter and more efficiently,” Benden said.

In a recent development, reference: “Improved Computer Utilization Associated with Height Adjustable Workstations in a Large Office Population” by Tricia Lynn Salzar, Matthew Lee Smith, Adam Pickens, Gang Han and Mark Edward Benden, 19 September 2026, Theoretical and Applied Ergonomics. DOI: 10.3390/tae2030021.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • To find out what coffee might be doing deep in the gut, researchers sent a tiny sensor through the digestive tract.
  • For many people, a morning cup of coffee does more than wake up the brain.
  • Researchers at the University of Copenhagen set out to investigate whether coffee drinking is linked to changes in gut function, particularly the muscle contractions that move food and waste through the digestive tract.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

To find out what coffee might be doing deep in the gut, researchers sent a tiny sensor through the digestive tract.

For many people, a morning cup of coffee does more than wake up the brain. It also seems to get the digestive system moving, sometimes sending them straight to the bathroom. But what exactly happens deep inside the intestines after regular coffee consumption?

Researchers at the University of Copenhagen set out to investigate whether coffee drinking is linked to changes in gut function, particularly the muscle contractions that move food and waste through the digestive tract. Understanding this connection could offer new insights into digestion and potentially point toward natural ways to relieve constipation.

To see what was happening inside the digestive tract, the team asked Danish volunteers to swallow a small electronic capsule. As it traveled, the capsule recorded temperature, pH, and intestinal contractions, along with how long it took to pass through.

It has been revealed that over the eight-day study, the researchers compared volunteers who drank one to five cups of coffee on at least four days with those who drank coffee less often. The frequent coffee drinkers had a wider variety of gut microorganisms, consistent with earlier research linking coffee intake to differences in the makeup of gut bacteria.

“But perhaps more importantly, frequent coffee consumption appears to affect the physiology of the gut itself, in other words, how the gut functions,” says first author Francesca Bucci, a PhD student in the University of Copenhagen’s Department of Nutrition, Exercise, and Sports. Earlier studies have linked moderate coffee intake to lower risks of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, depression, and several cancers. Its relationship with conditions inside the gut has received less attention.

Frequent coffee drinkers had a significantly lower pH in the small intestine, meaning it was more acidic. Higher coffee intake was also associated with more contractions in the colon.

“Contractions in the gut can support healthy digestion, help prevent constipation, and keep the intestinal muscles in good condition,” says Bucci.

The implications of the lower pH are less clear. Digestive enzymes work best within particular pH ranges, so changes in acidity can affect how they break down food. The researchers still need to determine what the difference means for health.

Industry observers note that because participants followed their usual coffee habits, the study could only identify links. Other differences between the groups may have contributed to the findings. Senior author Henrik Munch Roager, an associate professor and research group leader in the same department, points to earlier evidence that coffee can influence digestion.

In a recent development, “For example, we already know from other studies that coffee can influence a range of processes in the digestive system, including acid secretion in the stomach. So there are good reasons to believe that what we are seeing is not merely coincidence. Anecdotally, many people also report that coffee affects their digestion,” states Roager.

Recent findings suggest that roager proposes controlling how much coffee participants drink in a follow-up study. Comparing periods of high coffee intake with periods without coffee could help researchers pin down which changes are due to coffee itself.

It has been revealed that “A great many people struggle with constipation and irregular bowel movements. If we can understand how coffee affects digestion and intestinal contractions, it may be possible to use that knowledge to stimulate gut motility in a natural way. That would be extremely valuable,” claims Roager.

Reference: “Habitual coffee consumption is linked to differences in gut microbiota and gut physiology” by Francesca Bucci, Marie-Luise Puhlmann, Paula Rodriguez-Garcia, Xu Yujing, Jan Stanstrup, Jeroen Raes, Giorgia La Barbera, Nicola Procházková, Lars O. Dragsted, Martin F. Laursen and Henrik M. Roager, 15 September 2026, Gut Microbiology. DOI: 10.1016/j.gutmic.2026.100018.

Research Finds That Autistic Brains Are Far More Diverse Than Expected

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (601 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On average, autistic viewers’ brain responses more closely resembled those of non-autistic viewers than those of other autistic viewers while viewing movie scenes.
  • What happens in the brain when we watch a movie?
  • Sources indicate that in a study led by University of Iowa researchers Dorit Kliemann and James Traer, scientists examined functional MRI scans from 48 autistic adults and 90 non-autistic adults, collected at Indiana University and Caltech.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On average, autistic viewers’ brain responses more closely resembled those of non-autistic viewers than those of other autistic viewers while viewing movie scenes.

What happens in the brain when we watch a movie? As characters interact, emotions shift, and storylines unfold, our brains continuously interpret a complex stream of sights, sounds, and social cues. Scientists have long sought to understand how this process differs in autistic individuals, but newly introduced research suggests the answer may be far more complicated than previously thought.

Sources indicate that in a study led by University of Iowa researchers Dorit Kliemann and James Traer, scientists examined functional MRI scans from 48 autistic adults and 90 non-autistic adults, collected at Indiana University and Caltech. Their findings, published in The Journal of Neuroscience, reveal surprising similarities between the two groups while highlighting crucial differences that emerge when individual brain responses are examined.

It has been revealed that rather than relying on still images or simplified laboratory tasks, as many earlier studies have done, the researchers used six movie clips lasting five to 20 minutes each. The selections spanned animation, romantic comedy, action, and Hitchcockian thrillers, allowing the team to investigate how the brain responds as visual information, sounds, emotions, and social interactions unfold together in realistic, rapidly changing situations.

It has been revealed that the researchers trained a computer model to associate features of each clip with activity in different brain networks. Those features included what viewers saw and heard as well as subtler details, such as whether a scene had a positive or negative emotional tone.

“The computational model allowed us to look for robust brain responses to many different aspects of the complex, dynamic contexts in the movies,” Kliemann noted.

The model predicted brain activity better than chance across the clips and networks tested. It was most accurate in networks involved in hearing and language, and its average accuracy was similar in both groups.

The model’s predictions varied by about the same amount within a given person in either group. The difference emerged when the team compared one viewer with another. The patterns linking scenes to brain activity were more varied among autistic adults, with the biggest gap between groups appearing when the researchers analyzed social cues alone.

“We were surprised by the similarity of group averages. The results suggest that we need to focus on understanding the details of individual brain responses. How and why do they differ?” Traer noted.

In a recent development, the results point to substantial differences in how individual autistic adults’ brains respond to movies, particularly when processing social information. These differences were greater than those observed among non-autistic participants, even though the two groups revealed similar average brain responses. The findings suggest that understanding autism may require closer attention to individual patterns of brain activity rather than relying primarily on group averages.

The team now wants to find out when and where those differences appear in the brain and how they relate to differences in behavior. “Identifying ASD subgroups may help us build a more precise understanding of the condition and help develop ways to provide individually tailored support,” Kliemann said.

Sources indicate that reference: “Heterogeneous Encoding Patterns of Dynamic Audiovisual Social Stimuli in Autism Spectrum Disorder (Heterogeneous Encoding Patterns in Autism)” by Avery L. Van De Water, Lisa Byrge, Daniel P. Kennedy, Dorit Kliemann and James A. Traer, 14 November 2026, Journal of Neuroscience. DOI: 10.1523/JNEUROSCI.0055-26.2026.

This study was funded by NIH/National Institute of Mental Health, Iowa Initiative for Artificial Intelligence.

#42916. Scott Colom elected Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction

Scott Colom elected Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (756 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov.
  • Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen.
  • The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov. 4, has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. (Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images).

Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.

The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.

Industry observers note that colom was leading Hyde-Smith 49.2 percent to 48.7 percent — or by just over 4,600 votes out of more than 960,000 cast — when The Associated Press called the race Wednesday, a little over a week after Election Day. Ty Pinkins, the 2024 Democratic Senate nominee who ran as an independent this year, had 2 percent.

In recent days, as absentee and provisional ballots were counted, Colom had all but declared victory, repeatedly saying that Hyde-Smith had no path to victory.

“I'll work every day in the U.S. Senate to build a future that generations of Mississippians can be just as proud to call home,” he posted Monday on social media.

With his victory, Colom joins several other Democrats who flipped seats in deep-red states, including Texas’ James Talarico, Kansas’ Adam Hamilton and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews. Democrats have so far flipped eight Senate seats to win control of the chamber, overcoming a difficult Senate map and giving them their largest majority in the chamber since 2011.

That majority could expand further if Democrats flip the Senate seat in Alaska, where former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.

Recent findings suggest that republicans have dominated Senate elections in Mississippi in recent decades. The last Democrat to be elected senator in the Magnolia State was John C. Stennis, who won his sixth full and final term in 1982. Colom will be the third Black man to serve as a Mississippi senator after Republicans Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce during Reconstruction.

While Revels and Bruce, who left office in 1881, were elected by the state Legislature, Colom will be the first Black senator elected directly by voters.

Industry observers note that colom has served as a district attorney for four counties in northeast Mississippi since 2016. President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal district judgeship in 2022, but Hyde-Smith effectively blocked his nomination by not returning a so-called blue slip, a Senate Judiciary Committee tradition that lets senators derail district judge nominees in their home states.

Sources indicate that senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer said last week that he’d had Colom in his sights for several years as a potential Senate candidate, including for a race against the state’s senior senator, Republican Roger Wicker.

“I had Scott Colom and his father come to my house, and I served them a nice little brunch or something. I said, ‘You got to run,’” the Newly introduced York Democrat recalled to MS NOW. “They were smarter than me. This was four years ago. They said, ‘We don’t want to run this time, but we know that Hyde-[Smith], the incumbent, is so weak, we could beat her.’”.

Sources indicate that still, the Mississippi race didn’t capture as much national attention as other Senate contests until the closing weeks of the campaign. A trio of Black senators, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Cory Booker of Latest Jersey, all campaigned with Colom throughout the summer and fall. Key national figures, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, also stumped for him in October.

Industry observers note that colom’s campaign engaged voters with quirky ads and unconventional forms of outreach, including meeting with people lining up to attend a Trump rally. One ad that went viral played on Hyde Smith saying earlier this year that people had “so many proteins to choose from” when asked about rising beef prices.

According to recent reports, “Pick another protein?” says a man in the ad. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”.

Sources indicate that major Democratic outside groups made a late play in the state, with WinSenate, which is affiliated with Senate Democrats’ top super PAC, investing $2.2 million. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee spent $500,000 on a coordinated ad buy late last month.

In a recent development, the pro-Republican Senate Leadership Fund dropped $1.7 million on the race, and Trump headlined a rally for Hyde-Smith on Oct. 26.

#42915. Tech Report: Your City’s Sewage Could Be Hiding Secrets About Your Health, Scientists Discover

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (725 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scitechdaily ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Your City’s Sewage Could Be Hiding Secrets About Your Health, Scientists Discover

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (725 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bacteria flushed into sewers may offer clues to community health, with researchers finding links to chronic diseases and social conditions that could help reveal health disparities.
  • It has been revealed that during the COVID-19 pandemic, wastewater became an unexpected tool for protecting public health.
  • That success prompted researchers at The Ohio State University to consider a broader possibility: Could the same wastewater reveal something about chronic diseases, everyday health habits, and the conditions people live in?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bacteria flushed into sewers may offer clues to community health, with researchers finding links to chronic diseases and social conditions that could help reveal health disparities.

It has been revealed that during the COVID-19 pandemic, wastewater became an unexpected tool for protecting public health. By examining sewage for traces of viruses, scientists could monitor infections across entire communities.

That success prompted researchers at The Ohio State University to consider a broader possibility: Could the same wastewater reveal something about chronic diseases, everyday health habits, and the conditions people live in?

Sources indicate that “During the pandemic, the world learned how to use wastewater to track infectious disease. We asked, what else can it tell us?” remarked Emma Lancaster, lead author of a study published in the journal Environmental Research.

Lancaster began exploring that question while working with samples collected for COVID-19 surveillance. A former doctoral student in Ohio State’s College of Public Health, she now works as an environmental health consultant in Boston.

According to recent reports, her idea centered on the bacteria that normally live in the human gut. Some of these microbes end up in wastewater, where they can offer clues about the collective gut microbiome of a community. Because gut bacteria can vary alongside health and lifestyle, the researchers wanted to see whether differences in wastewater bacteria reflected broader public health patterns.

According to recent reports, to investigate, the team analyzed 27 wastewater samples collected in 2022 from nine treatment plants serving eight Ohio cities. Together, these urban and rural communities were home to more than 1.3 million people. The researchers identified bacteria associated with the human gut and compared their findings with publicly available information on chronic diseases, health behaviors, demographics, and socioeconomic conditions.

It has been revealed that the results showed distinct bacterial profiles across the cities. Several types of bacteria were associated with community rates of obesity, high blood pressure, asthma, and other chronic conditions. The researchers also found connections with smoking, depression, physical activity, and unemployment.

One bacterial group, called Desulfovibrio, stood out because its abundance was associated with eight different health measures, including obesity, high blood pressure, stroke, and other chronic diseases.

Sources indicate that rural communities generally had more of these bacteria, along with higher rates of several chronic health conditions. The findings suggested that wastewater might help researchers investigate health differences between communities, including disparities that are not fully explained by existing public health data.

“In many cases, poor health outcomes are worse in rural areas, and to see these distinct indicators of poorer gut microbiome health in these rural areas offers us clues to some of what is driving that,” Lancaster said.

Sources indicate that these associations do not establish that the bacteria caused the health problems. Rather, they provide potential indicators that researchers can investigate further. By identifying patterns across communities, wastewater monitoring could eventually help public officials recognize areas facing greater health challenges and make more informed decisions about where to direct resources.

“Wastewater offers a unique way to understand the health of whole communities, not just the people who show up in clinics,” said Jiyoung Lee, professor and chair of environmental health sciences at Ohio State and the study’s senior author.

The approach builds on an established form of infectious disease surveillance, although using it to understand chronic health conditions remains an emerging possibility.

“It already helps us track viruses including those that cause COVID, flu and Mpox, and it has potential to support investigations of foodborne illness, such as the recent Cyclospora outbreak,” Lee mentioned.

The researchers believe wastewater could eventually help communities evaluate public health initiatives, not simply identify where health problems are more common. One possibility involves monitoring changes in gut bacteria to investigate whether programs intended to improve nutrition are having the desired effects.

“Now, our findings suggest its value could extend beyond infectious agents — for example, tracking community gut microbiome changes could eventually help us assess whether nutrition programs are improving gut health.”.

It has been revealed that reference: “Wastewater-based human gut microbiome surveillance links microbial signatures to population health in Ohio communities” by Emma Lancaster and Jiyoung Lee, 15 September 2026, Environmental Research. DOI: 10.1016/j.envres.2026.125332.

This work was partially funded by the Ohio Department of Health.

Breaking: The brain’s fear center moonlights as the save button for memories

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (611 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.
  • Recent findings suggest that neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.

Recent findings suggest that neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience. Though the study doesn’t nail down the exact mechanism for memory formation, it points to a broader role for the amygdala within the memory-sorting apparatus.

Industry observers note that the study probes an enduring quandary about the mind, states neuroscientist Jiayang Xiao of Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University in Los Angeles. “We forget much of what we experience … only a fraction of the information we encounter becomes a lasting memory,” she says.

Although a role for the amygdala in memory has been suggested before, previous studies that used electrodes reading brain activity through the scalp, or at the scale of thousands rather than individual neurons, captured a blurrier picture. It’s akin to a microphone recording from outside of a stadium, says cognitive neuroscientist Cory Inman at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, who was not involved in the study.

“You might be able to tell that there’s a game happening. You might be able to tell when somebody scores a touchdown. You might even be able to tell that one side of the stadium is cheering for one team and another side of the stadium is cheering for another team,” but that’s about it, Inman says. The new study is more like a lapel mic pinned on a single fan in terms of scale and what the researchers were able to capture, adding clarity.

The amygdala, which is typically associated with regulating emotions like fear and aggression, has neurons that are challenging to reach, residing in two clusters deep within the brain. Xiao and her colleagues leveraged electrodes previously surgically implanted in more than 90 people with drug-resistant epilepsy to identify where seizures originate. In their new role, the electrodes singled out neurons involved in saving memories.

Patients were shown images of everyday objects belonging to five categories such as food and animals. About 10 to 30 minutes later, they attempted to recall which images were already shown. Xiao and her colleagues found that activity in certain amygdala neurons corresponded with an image being remembered. The image had been earmarked for longer term storage, Xiao indicates.

Although participants had to recall something from half an hour ago at most and the exact mechanism for saving memories is still unclear, the researchers think there are two main steps of the process. The team indicated that individual neurons have a preference for one of the five categories of images. First the image is categorized by the amygdala. Then, the strength of the category neuron response the first time the image is shown dictates whether the image is later recalled.

A better understanding of this mechanism may pave the way for more effective treatments of memory disorders, Xiao says, a medical conundrum for which there are at the moment no broadly effective treatments.

According to recent reports, the hippocampus is typically more directly linked to memory, so “it surprised me that we observe such a clear relationship between memory formation and activity in the amygdala,” Xiao says. By contrast, the correlation between hippocampus neuron activity and image recall was weaker and slightly delayed.

Future work like observing the impacts of stimulating amygdala neurons on memory will help researchers discern if this region can be targeted to improve memory, Xiao says.

For now, the secret to memory’s hidden machinations remains in the shadows.

#42911. On the Brink of Extinction, These Giant Sea Turtles Are Doing Something Unexpected

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (901 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scitechdaily ↗ Open Full Page

On the Brink of Extinction, These Giant Sea Turtles Are Doing Something Unexpected

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (901 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A sea turtle population that has declined by more than 90% is showing encouraging nesting success in Ecuador, where cooler ocean conditions coincide with more nests.
  • Industry observers note that when a critically endangered leatherback sea turtle named Bella came ashore in Ecuador in January 2026, her search for a nesting spot took an unexpected turn.
  • Bella eventually returned to the ocean without nesting, but two nights later, she tried again on a quieter stretch of beach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A sea turtle population that has declined by more than 90% is showing encouraging nesting success in Ecuador, where cooler ocean conditions coincide with more nests.

Industry observers note that when a critically endangered leatherback sea turtle named Bella came ashore in Ecuador in January 2026, her search for a nesting spot took an unexpected turn. Confused by nearby streetlights, she climbed over a rock breakwater at Playa de Crucita and ended up on a sidewalk instead of the sandy beach where she needed to lay her eggs.

Bella eventually returned to the ocean without nesting, but two nights later, she tried again on a quieter stretch of beach. This time, she successfully buried 47 eggs in the sand. A few weeks later, 44 baby turtles emerged and made their way toward the sea.

Sources indicate that her persistence is part of a potentially hopeful development for the eastern Pacific leatherback, a critically endangered population of the world’s largest sea turtle. During the 2025–2026 nesting season, researchers documented a record number of leatherback nests along several beaches in Ecuador, more than 1,000 miles from the turtles’ traditional nesting grounds in Mexico and Costa Rica.

The findings raise an intriguing possibility. As ocean temperatures change, some leatherbacks may be adjusting where they reproduce, taking advantage of cooler conditions along Ecuador’s coast. Whether this represents a lasting adaptation remains uncertain, but successful nesting in new locations could offer opportunities for a population that has declined dramatically.

“Historically, observing female Eastern Pacific leatherbacks on Ecuador’s beaches was a rare or unusual event, but our findings suggest they are adapting their reproductive cycle to thrive and survive in coastal Ecuador,” says Juan José Alava, a marine ecotoxicologist, adjunct professor at Simon Fraser University’s School of Resource and Environmental Management, and leading co-author of the study.

In a study published in Chelonian Conservation and Biology, researchers examined more than 45 years of records documenting reproductive-age female turtles, nesting attempts, nests, hatching success, and stranded turtles along Ecuador’s coastline. They compared these observations with El Niño and La Niña events, which bring warmer and cooler ocean conditions.

Over the past decade, the records revealed increased leatherback activity and nesting during cooler La Niña periods in the southeastern tropical Pacific. This relationship suggests that ocean temperatures may influence where females lay their eggs, although the findings do not establish that warming waters are directly causing them to move.

The Ecuadorian nests also revealed encouraging results. The number of eggs per nest and the proportion that successfully hatched were comparable to those recorded at traditional nesting sites farther north. In some cases, Alava says, Ecuadorian nests produced more hatchlings than usual.

It has been revealed that leatherbacks are particularly well suited to life across dramatically different ocean environments. They are the only sea turtles that thrive in both warm and cold conditions, traveling thousands of miles between tropical nesting beaches and subpolar Pacific feeding grounds, where they feast on jellyfish during the summer. Their extensive travels have even brought them to Canada’s west coast, with more than 150 records from British Columbia waters between 1931 and 2024.

Despite that remarkable flexibility, eastern Pacific leatherbacks have suffered a population decline of more than 90 percent since the 1980s. Their survival is threatened by unusually warm El Niño conditions, which are worsened by human-caused climate change, as well as fishing bycatch, plastic pollution, vessel strikes, egg harvesting, and the loss of nesting habitat.

“It signals fresh hope for a subspecies of leatherback on track for extinction in the eastern Pacific within 60 years. They are making their way alongside nature against all odds, representing hope for this species and other sea turtle species even as they reach tipping points.”.

It has been revealed that bella’s nesting success offers one example of what Ecuador’s beaches could provide. After researchers tagged her during her first unsuccessful attempt, they discovered that she nested four to five times in 2026 alone. One nest was left in its original location, while the others were moved to the San Jacinto hatchery.

Across the season, Bella laid 146 eggs, producing 134 hatchlings for an overall success rate of 91.8 percent.

It has been revealed that yet finding suitable nesting beaches is only part of the challenge. Bella’s encounter with streetlights and a coastal barrier illustrates how human activity can interfere with reproduction, even when turtles reach a promising location.

Alava emphasizes that continued monitoring, efforts to reduce accidental capture in fishing operations, and effective management of Ecuador’s nesting beaches will be essential to protecting the population over the long term. He also stresses the importance of involving coastal communities in conservation decisions.

“Management and conservation efforts should be championed in close consultation and participation with local and traditional ecological knowledge through coastal, community-grounded interventions.”.

Recent findings suggest that reference: “A New Hope: Eastern Pacific Leatherback (Dermochelys coriacea) Nesting and Stranding Observations Amidst a Warming Ocean Show the Value of Ecuador for Species Persistence” by Juan José Alava, Kerly Briones, Cristian Soledispa, Cristina Miranda, Eduardo Espinoza, Johanna Moreira, Jodie J. Darquea, Felipe Vallejo, Juan F. Pesántez-Muñoz, Jacqueline Sócola, Johnny Moreira, Carlos Cruz, Marlon Intriago, Kevin Reyes, Alan Miranda, Raúl Carvajal, Cyntia Mizobe, Pedro Jiménez, Nikita Gaibor, Nastenka Calle and María José Barragán-Paladines, 19 October 2026, Chelonian Conservation and Biology. DOI: 10.2744/CCB-1686.1.

#42910. Why Did Early Humans Collect Strange Stones 500,000 Years Ago? Scientists Have a New Theory

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (903 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scitechdaily ↗ Open Full Page

Why Did Early Humans Collect Strange Stones 500,000 Years Ago? Scientists Have a New Theory

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (903 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Prehistoric discoveries in Israel raise the possibility that keeping meaningful objects helped early humans distinguish personal memories from stories and gradually develop a sense of identity.
  • A stone picked up during a hike or a seashell brought home from the beach might seem ordinary to everyone else.
  • A new study from Tel Aviv University suggests that early humans may have collected and kept objects for much the same reason we do today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prehistoric discoveries in Israel raise the possibility that keeping meaningful objects helped early humans distinguish personal memories from stories and gradually develop a sense of identity.

A stone picked up during a hike or a seashell brought home from the beach might seem ordinary to everyone else. Yet years later, that small object can bring back memories of where you were, who you were with, and what made the experience special. It’s a familiar human habit, and researchers now believe its origins may reach back nearly half a million years.

A new study from Tel Aviv University suggests that early humans may have collected and kept objects for much the same reason we do today. The researchers propose that these prehistoric keepsakes could have helped shape our ability to remember personal experiences and develop a sense of who we are.

The idea emerged from archaeological discoveries at several prehistoric sites in Israel, where researchers found colorful stones, unusual handaxes, and much older tools that appeared to have been collected despite offering no obvious practical benefit.

According to recent reports, at Qesem Cave, for example, small, colorful pebbles had been brought in from different locations. In the Sakhnin Valley, handaxes were made from flint containing fossils or unusual geological patterns. Some were carefully shaped so that these distinctive features remained at the center, where they could be seen and touched.

Other discoveries offer an intriguing connection to the past. At Revadim, Jaljulia, and Qesem Cave, researchers identified older flint tools that had apparently been collected after their surfaces had changed with age. Although some were resharpened, much of their original surfaces and evidence of earlier workmanship remained intact.

Why would someone keep an old tool when they could make a upcoming one? The researchers suggest that its age and appearance may have been part of its appeal. Just as an old family heirloom can carry meaning beyond its usefulness, these objects might have been valued for the experiences or histories associated with them.

Recent findings suggest that dr. Yoav Ram of Tel Aviv University’s School of Zoology explains the possibility:.

“When early humans brought a colorful stone or an old tool they had found in the landscape back to their cave, that object may have helped them remember a significant event or encounter for the rest of their lives. In this way, keepsakes may have become a kind of ‘external memory device,’ supporting the evolution of brain mechanisms responsible for autobiographical memory, which is so characteristic of us as humans and so important in shaping our identity.”.

There may be a deeper psychological reason why such objects mattered. Our minds do not simply store experiences. They must also distinguish between things we personally experienced, stories we heard from others, and events we imagined.

Sources indicate that the researchers propose that seeing or touching a familiar object could have helped early humans make those distinctions. A stone collected from a particular location, for instance, might have brought back a personal memory of being there.

Recent findings suggest that that ability could have mattered well beyond individual recollection. Remembering encounters, alliances, gifts, mutual obligations, and rights connected to particular places helps people maintain relationships and cooperate. A keepsake could also be carried elsewhere and shown to others, potentially making a personal account more convincing and helping establish trust.

The researchers believe this behavior may have become especially useful as early humans faced changes in their environment.

Prof. Ran Barkai offers one possible explanation:.

“The disappearance of large animals, particularly elephants, required early humans to develop latest hunting methods and become familiar with hunting grounds inhabited by animals such as fallow deer and wild cattle. Objects taken from these places may have helped them maintain a personal connection with the places that would henceforth provide their livelihood.”.

Over many generations, the researchers suggest, keeping meaningful objects may have placed evolutionary pressure on the brain systems involved in identifying where memories come from and how reliable they are.

Sources indicate that in this proposed scenario, objects and memory evolved together. As people increasingly used physical reminders of their experiences, the brain mechanisms supporting personal memory may have become more sophisticated.

Recent findings suggest that that process could have contributed to the development of autobiographical memory, our ability to connect individual experiences into a continuing story of our lives. It is an key part of how we understand our identities and our relationships with others.

According to recent reports, the researchers emphasize that their interpretation remains a hypothesis. An unusual stone or carefully preserved tool does not necessarily prove that its owner associated it with a personal memory. The archaeological evidence cannot reveal exactly what someone was thinking hundreds of thousands of years ago.

However, the findings suggest that the habit of keeping meaningful objects may date back roughly 500,000 years, long before written records or photographs.

And if the researchers’ interpretation is correct, the simple act of keeping a stone from a memorable place may once have played a role in the evolution of how humans remember their lives.

Industry observers note that reference: “Homo Memorabiliaxis: Souvenirs and the Evolution of Autobiographical Memory and Self” by Ran Barkai, Ella Assaf, Bar Efrati, Tal Simon, Liad Mudrik and Yoav Ram, 19 October 2026, Evolutionary Anthropology: Issues, News, and Reviews. DOI: 10.1002/evan.70051.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, president Donald Trump speaks with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct.
  • President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.
  • It has been revealed that on the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the upcoming Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, president Donald Trump speaks with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct. 13 before leaving for a campaign rally in Alaska. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.

It has been revealed that on the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the upcoming Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill. But on the other, he promoted his hard-line aide Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff, raising doubts about any cooling of the political environment.

At every stop along his October campaign rally blitz before Republicans suffered massive losses on Nov. 3, Trump railed against “Dumbocrats” and their “bad” policies. He mocked their candidates as too extreme, too corrupt and too beholden to the most progressive wing of their party. He even warned that, if voters handed them control of the House and Senate, it would set off “a 1929-style economic depression.”.

Voters ignored him. They handed House Democrats over 250 seats at least come January, and the party will have at least 54 seats in the Senate.

In a recent development, trump was asked during a “60 Minutes” interview taped Friday afternoon at the White House if he could resist insulting Democratic lawmakers for six months if that’s how long it took to reach a deal on major legislation. “Very easily,” he responded.

But several Democrats are so sure about getting to a “Kumbaya” moment with Trump during his final two years.

Recent findings suggest that virginia Sen. Tim Kaine stated it was hard to take the president at his word because he is “so unpredictable.”.

“But I'm certainly telling my colleagues we should try to put as many bills as we can on his desk that do good things for the American public, and then see how he behaves,” he noted Tuesday.

Recent findings suggest that "We're gonna put bills in front of the president on affordability starting Day One,” California Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely incoming House Oversight and Government Reform chair, remarked Tuesday. “We'll have to see if he's serious, but I don't trust Donald Trump for a second.”.

The White House on Monday sent Garcia a letter, obtained by CQ Roll Call, warning House Democrats that their anticipated spate of probes "may cross the line into blatant criminality.".

Rep. Jim McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat who is in line to chair the Rules Committee in the upcoming Congress, noted on the floor Tuesday that he does not see a GOP that is ready to heed the election's lessons and come to the bargaining table.

“Instead of taking the hint or listening to the overwhelming majority of Americans who told them to change course, Republicans are doubling down on the same tactics and messaging they've been jamming down our throats these last two years, and it's a perfect example of why they lost in the first place,” he remarked. “They do not listen.

It has been revealed that “Then to double down even further, the failed lame-duck president appointed Stephen Miller, the architect of all the cruel policies that most people hate, as his upcoming White House chief of staff,” McGovern added, referring to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. “What planet are these people living on?”.

Kaine said congressional Democrats might not notice that much of a change from the White House with Miller moving into the chief’s suite near the Oval Office.

Recent findings suggest that “Stephen Miller was calling a lot of the shots, even if he wasn't chief of staff,” the Virginia Democrat said. “So I view that as a kind of a change of the face, but not of the character of the administration.”.

House Republicans’ Tuesday vote to make hard-line conservative Jim Jordan of Ohio their next leader is another red flag for Democrats.

Sources indicate that “White House Chief of staff Stephen Miller and House Minority Leader Jim Jordan,” Brendan Duke, a former senior Democratic Senate aide now with the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, wrote on X. “Where is the pivot to the center after a historic election loss?”.

Sources indicate that getting to the center is what retiring Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon says his fellow Republicans and Trump should be doing after the election massacre.

According to recent reports, "I do wish we could get to the point where we could solve significant problems, instead of just beating the other side,” said Bacon, who has floated a 2028 presidential bid. “We can’t do this Republican-only or Democrat-only. And I would say this to the president, too: We’ve got to start working across the aisle to solve these problems.”.

It has been revealed that despite his postelection talk of working with Democrats, Trump has sought to blame them for an up-and-down U.S. stock market.

“Right after the election it went down $3 trillion,” he remarked Monday during an unplanned White House press briefing. “That was because of the result of the election, because the stock market does not want to see Democrats. And your 401(k)s have gone way down because of the ridiculous result.”.

In a recent development, he's also returned this week to questioning the midterm results: “It's not even a result. It's almost hard to believe. Now, I wasn't on the ballot.”.

Recent findings suggest that members of House Republicans’ fresh leadership team on Tuesday sounded dug in and ready for a partisan brawl over Democrats’ promised investigations into the president, many of his top aides and Trump family members. Jordan's election as GOP leader shows that “we are ready to dig in for the fight,” outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters Tuesday.

According to recent reports, michigan Rep. Lisa McClain, who was reelected House GOP conference chair, pointed to Garcia's two-word statement on Election Day: "Lawyer up.".

Industry observers note that “Tell me how ‘lawyering up’ helps anybody with affordability?" she remarked. “They're going to be focused on going after President Trump. We are going to be focused on improving the quality of life for every American.”.

To that end, retiring Maryland Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, a former No. 2 House Democrat, noted Republicans should heed one substantial takeaway from the election: “Trump lost.”.
