💡 Key Takeaways
  • New guidance explains how first periods, pregnancy complications, and menopause can offer clues to a woman’s heart disease risk.
  • Picture a heart attack and you probably picture a man in his fifties clutching his chest.
  • It has been revealed that yet heart disease kills more women in the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New guidance explains how first periods, pregnancy complications, and menopause can offer clues to a woman’s heart disease risk.

Picture a heart attack and you probably picture a man in his fifties clutching his chest.

It has been revealed that yet heart disease kills more women in the U.S. than breast cancer and lung cancer combined, and much of what sets a woman’s risk happens decades before menopause.

New joint guidance from four medical societies tells doctors to start reading that risk at a girl’s first period.

The guidance comes as three papers from the American Heart Association, the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.

It’s built from existing evidence rather than a fresh trial, so it reorganizes what doctors already know instead of adding a new finding.

Industry observers note that sadiya Khan, a cardiologist at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine, chaired the writing group. In an interview with Earth.com, she compared it to saving money.

Industry observers note that “You would never wait until retirement to start saving. We should bring that same thinking to heart health,” Khan noted.

Standard cardiovascular risk calculators already account for sex, but they don’t capture every risk factor tied to a woman’s reproductive history.

Sources indicate that the latest framework splits a woman’s life into four stages set by her hormones. They are the years around the first period, the decades of regular cycles, the transition into menopause, and the years after it.

Pregnancy counts as a separate event, running from 12 months before conception to 12 months after delivery.

Estrogen and progesterone act on blood vessels, heart muscle and the brain, not only on the reproductive organs.

Because those hormones rise and fall about once a month, with no equivalent in men, blood vessel function and sleep vary in the same rhythm.

The authors wrote that risk in each stage is shaped by the stages before it.

Asked by Earth.com which stage is most overlooked, Khan said the biggest gaps are what happened earlier, such as irregular or heavy periods, pregnancy complications and a diagnosis like endometriosis.

Those shape heart health in later stages, she noted, and belong in the conversation at every visit.

“Heart health for women doesn’t start at menopause,” said Amanda Perak, a pediatric cardiologist at Lurie Children’s Hospital of Chicago who worked on all three papers. “Puberty is a big turning point.”.

A first period before age 10 is linked to higher heart disease risk later in life, and the 2026 cholesterol guideline already lists it as a risk enhancer.

According to recent reports, some irregularity is normal in the first one to three years. A pattern that persists can signal the hormone disorder that used to be called polycystic ovary syndrome, which often comes with insulin resistance and unhealthy cholesterol.

The disorder, now called polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, affects an estimated 10% to 13% of women.

According to recent reports, heavy periods affect 20% to 30% of young women, and about half of those with heavy bleeding are low on iron. The authors wrote that menstrual patterns may be the earliest sign of heart risk a doctor can see.

Mental health turns in the same years. By about age 17, girls have at least twice the odds of a depression diagnosis as boys.

Teens with depression are more likely to develop obesity later, and the reverse holds too. Nearly one in five girls in organized sports consider quitting over menstrual concerns, the authors wrote.

“The goal isn’t to worry teens about the chance of a heart attack, which are decades away for nearly all of them,” Perak mentioned.

“It’s that the teen years are when patterns get set, and it’s much easier to keep good heart health than to get it back.”.

Estrogen levels in pregnancy rise to about 30 times their peak in a normal cycle, and the heart and metabolism both change to support the fetus.

The authors call it a stress test because it can expose risk that was already there.

Nearly nine in ten women ages 20 to 44 begin pregnancy with less-than-ideal heart health.

High blood pressure in pregnancy, gestational diabetes and preterm birth are each linked to higher heart disease risk later in life.

Mood and anxiety disorders affect up to 37% of women in the first three months after delivery.

The year after a birth is a vulnerable time for follow-up. Women move from obstetric care back to primary care, and that handoff is often missed.

The guidance notes that the obstetric threshold for hypertension, a systolic reading of at least 140 or a diastolic reading of at least 90, matches the cutoff for stage 2 hypertension in general adult care.

Perimenopause begins at a median age of about 47 in the U.S., and the authors describe it as a period of swings rather than a steady decline.

In a recent development, LDL, the so-called bad cholesterol, rises during the transition independent of aging. Hot flashes affect 50% to 80% of women in this stage, and about one in three report significant depression or anxiety symptoms.

Women then spend about 40% of their lives after menopause. Around 67 million American women are 50 or older, and an estimated 6,000 more reach menopause every day.

Menopause that arrives early carries extra heart risk of its own.

Hormone therapy can help manage menopause symptoms, but the authors advise against using it to prevent heart disease.

Sources indicate that years of unhealthy habits may begin to show in this stage as heart disease. Stacey Rosen, the association’s immediate past volunteer president, noted it is never too late to do something about it.

“It’s always about opportunities,” Rosen said.

A woman may see a pediatrician, a primary care doctor, an obstetrician, a cardiologist and a psychologist over her life, and their notes rarely travel with her.

One of the three papers surveyed 70 leaders of women’s cardiovascular centers and heard back from 33.

Of those programs, 29 are in cities and one is rural, and the paper proposes a national network of centers that combine the specialties.

Khan told Earth.com the papers are a first step toward giving every clinician the same playbook.

The next change, she mentioned, is connecting all the clinicians on a woman’s care team through the life stage framework.

Her advice for the next appointment was a single question. “Ask at every life stage: What is my heart risk, and what should I do about it now? It is never too early to talk about your heart health,” she stated.

The framework rests on evidence that links these stages to risk, and the papers say plainly where the links are weakest.

It isn’t known whether treating severe hot flashes lowers heart disease risk, with or without hormones. Female-specific cutoffs for heart imaging tests aren’t yet in guidelines.

And none of the three papers reports a trial showing that sorting care by life stage, rather than by age, prevents more heart attacks and strokes.

Khan mentioned she is especially interested in reaching younger women now that risk can be estimated up to 30 years ahead with the association’s PREVENT equations.

Whether clinics can be rebuilt around that forecast is the test the four societies have set themselves.

The research was published in the journal Circulation.

It has been revealed that more U.S. women are taking menopause hormone therapy, newly introduced prescription data suggest.

Monthly dispensing of hormone therapy for women aged 40 to 74 more than doubled since 2023, growing from 2 million to 4.9 million, researchers report November 19 in JAMA. The analysis of U.S. pharmacy dispensing data revealed that this increase began in 2024. The rise continued in 2025, before and after the Food and Drug Administration’s November removal of the black box warning from packaging, and into 2026.

Although the data in the latest study are aggregate, the researchers used population data to estimate the dispensing rate for this age group, which jumped from 28 prescriptions per 1,000 women to 67 prescriptions per 1,000 over the period studied.

It’s possible that the evidence regarding hormone therapy’s safety and effectiveness for the treatment of menopause symptoms, such as hot flashes, is reaching more women. Medical groups such as the Menopause Society have recommended menopause hormone therapy for women with symptoms who are younger than 60 or within 10 years of the start of menopause, absent certain risk factors including prior breast cancer and stroke.

It has been revealed that “Greater attention to women’s health, updated medical guidance supporting individualized menopause hormone therapy and social media may all be contributing to increased interest,” says Dana Sarnak, who studies sexual and reproductive health at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine. Anecdotally, her clinician colleagues report more patients seeking menopause care, she says.

Many women and physicians turned away from hormone therapy in the early 2000s after a large study called the Women’s Health Initiative raised safety concerns, which were later considered overblown. Research since then has provided a more nuanced understanding of the benefits and risks of menopause hormone therapy at different ages.

There are safer formulations, including patches and gels, of estrogen today then at the time of the Women’s Health Initiative, for which participants took a pill. The latest study found that product use increased for transdermal and vaginal estrogen and for progesterone products — women who have their uterus need to take progesterone along with estrogen. The use of oral formulations remained stable. There has been a shortage of estrogen patches in the United States this year, which the U.S. Food and Drug Administration attributes to increasing demand.

#42828. Why did Earth stay hot for millions of years? Fossil shells offer a clue

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (947 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Why did Earth stay hot for millions of years? Fossil shells offer a clue

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (947 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A weaker carbon pump in the Southern Ocean may explain about half of the rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide during an ancient warm period.
  • The Southern Ocean helps move carbon from the atmosphere into the deep sea.
  • Around 50 million years ago, during one of Earth’s warmest periods in the past 66 million years, that process appears to have weakened.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A weaker carbon pump in the Southern Ocean may explain about half of the rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide during an ancient warm period.

The Southern Ocean helps move carbon from the atmosphere into the deep sea.

Around 50 million years ago, during one of Earth’s warmest periods in the past 66 million years, that process appears to have weakened.

Chemical traces in fossil shells suggest that microscopic plants at the ocean’s surface used a smaller share of the nutrients available to them than they did in cooler periods before and after.

That left more carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, according to the study’s model.

The model suggests that the weaker carbon pump and the feedbacks it amplified could explain about half of the rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide at the time.

Simone Moretti of the Max Planck Institute for Chemistry in Mainz, Germany, led the study. His co-authors came from the Université libre de Bruxelles (ULB), the University of California, Santa Cruz and other institutions.

“Our study reveals that the Southern Ocean played a major role in regulating atmospheric CO2 during the early Eocene, millions of years before the onset of the recent ice ages,” Moretti mentioned.

The Early Eocene Climatic Optimum ran from about 53 to 49 million years ago. Global temperatures were more than 18°F (10°C) higher than now, and carbon dioxide reached around 1,600 parts per million.

The causes of those levels are still debated. Volcanoes and reduced burial of organic carbon have both been proposed, but the timing of the eruptions lines up poorly with the warming.

So the team looked at the ocean’s biological carbon pump. Microscopic plants near the surface take up carbon dioxide as they grow. When they die, some of that carbon sinks and stays in the deep ocean for hundreds to thousands of years.

Today the pump runs below its full potential. Deep water rising around Antarctica brings up nutrients that the plants never fully use.

Sources indicate that plankton prefer the lighter form of nitrogen when they take up nitrate, their main nutrient. The more completely they use the supply, the heavier the leftover nitrogen becomes.

Sources indicate that the nitrogen signature ends up in the shells of foraminifera, single-celled organisms that eat the plankton. The team measured the nitrogen trapped in fossil foraminifera from four sediment cores drilled by the Ocean Drilling Program.

Two cores came from the Southern Ocean. Two came from the mid-latitude Atlantic and Indian oceans, where nutrients are used up almost completely.

The gap between the two pairs of sites shows how much nutrient the Southern Ocean plants left behind. It was widest exactly when temperatures and carbon dioxide peaked, and it narrowed or vanished before and after.

The team then ran a simple model of the ocean and atmosphere using the estimated 40% drop in the share of available nutrients that plankton used.

On its own, the drop raised carbon dioxide from 700 to about 900 parts per million.

When the researchers included the effects of warming and changes in seawater chemistry, atmospheric carbon dioxide reached about 1,100 parts per million.

That increase accounts for about half of the roughly 800 parts per million rise reconstructed for the period.

The leak hit harder than it would today. Eocene seawater was more acidic and richer in calcium, so it had less capacity to absorb a change in carbon dioxide.

“Because Eocene seawater had a much lower capacity to buffer changes in CO2 than today’s ocean, a weakening of the biological carbon pump could have had a far greater impact on atmospheric CO2 than under present-day conditions,” remarked François Fripiat, a co-author at ULB.

Over millions of years, rain and rock weathering normally pull carbon dioxide back out of the air and act as a thermostat.

The early Eocene had no Alps or Himalayas yet, and its flat, deeply weathered continents offered little fresh rock.

“With Earth’s natural thermostat operating less efficiently, the additional CO2 released from the ocean could remain in the atmosphere for much longer,” said Mathis Hain, a co-author at the University of California, Santa Cruz.

“This would allow the Southern Ocean to influence climate not just over thousands of years, as during the ice ages, but over millions of years,” he noted.

The Southern Ocean also released carbon dioxide during warm spells between recent ice ages.

The authors interpret the match across very different timescales as a sign of a dependable feedback.

According to recent reports, the shells record that the plants left nutrients unused, but not why. Stronger mixing around Antarctica could have brought up more deep water, or the plants could have grown less.

The authors argued that iron supply, which limits plant growth there today, likely changed little in a warmer world. That leaves less room for the growth explanation.

The estimate of the nutrient drop is deliberately conservative, because one of the mid-latitude sites falls between the others in its values.

And the carbon model is a simple one, built to show the size of the effect rather than reproduce the Eocene ocean.

The open question is whether the modern Southern Ocean will respond the same way.

Simulations run for centuries to thousands of years suggest deep-water formation near Antarctica strengthens once the deep ocean catches up with surface warming, which would match the Eocene pattern.

The team is now exploring the same feedback in other periods of sustained warming. The paper names the Middle Eocene, the Middle Miocene and the Pliocene as candidates.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Geoscience.

#42826. What can AI learn from a thousand days of hearing what a baby hears?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1288 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

What can AI learn from a thousand days of hearing what a baby hears?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1288 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Princeton recorded eight babies for their first 1,000 days, and a model trained on one child's audio learned language on the same schedule.
  • It has been revealed that A toddler can pick up hundreds of words just by hearing people talk.
  • Researchers at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute wired up 15 homes with cameras and microphones and recorded babies for most of their waking hours across the first 1,000 days of life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Princeton recorded eight babies for their first 1,000 days, and a model trained on one child's audio learned language on the same schedule.

It has been revealed that A toddler can pick up hundreds of words just by hearing people talk. Could a computer start from scratch and recognize many of those same words on roughly the same timetable?

Researchers at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute wired up 15 homes with cameras and microphones and recorded babies for most of their waking hours across the first 1,000 days of life.

The researchers turned speech recorded around eight children into clean audio using synthetic voices.

They trained a separate model on each child’s audio in the order the speech was originally recorded.

The models identified recurring sound patterns that corresponded to words.

On average, each model reached the halfway point on a vocabulary checklist within 22 days of the child it was paired with.

“We wanted to turn the usual logic of developmental research around,” mentioned Uri Hasson, a professor of psychology and neuroscience at Princeton who led the study.

“Instead of observing a child for an hour in the laboratory, we asked whether we could build a model capable of learning and immerse it in the child’s actual experience, day after day.”.

It has been revealed that the families were in New Jersey and spanned a range of incomes and backgrounds. Each home got four to 14 recording devices spread across two to five rooms.

The devices ran 12 to 14 hours a day, from February 2022 to May 2025.

Recent findings suggest that the project gathered roughly 1.2 million hours of audio and video, of which the eight homes analyzed in this paper supplied about 600,000. An automated pipeline worked out where the child was in the house and pulled out the speech happening nearby.

Each child ended up with between 1,900 and 6,600 hours of usable speech, three to seven and a half hours a day. That adds up to 6 to 27 million words per child, over a median of 960 recording days.

It has been revealed that every month from eight months on, caregivers filled out a standard checklist of which words their child understood and stated. Those forms are how the researchers knew what each child knew, and when.

Children reached half of the 649-word checklist anywhere from about 12 to 22 months old. That ten-month spread between children is the thing most studies average away.

The model started from random numbers. It had no dictionary, no phonetics, no notion of where one word ends and the next begins, and no text.

The program’s first part chops the incoming sound into 20-millisecond pieces and sorts them into categories it invents for itself. Its second part tries to guess the next piece from what came before.

Whenever a run of pieces becomes reliably predictable, the program files it away as a unit, which is the closest thing it has to a word.

Recent findings suggest that nothing about that design is specific to English or even to speech. What makes it unusual is the schedule.

The audio arrives in the order it was recorded, one day at a time, rather than shuffled into batches the way an AI language model is normally trained.

At the end of each simulated day, the program gets a sample of speech from earlier days, weighted toward recent ones. The researchers call it replay.

English has 39 phonemes, the sound units that distinguish bat from pat. Children spend their first year tuning in to the ones their own language uses.

Within roughly 12 to 15 months of simulated time, the program had carved out dedicated categories for nearly all of them.

According to recent reports, across the eight children, the models averaged 37.5 phonemes each. The lowest count came from the household with the least recording.

The order it happened in, sounds before words, is the order infants follow.

According to recent reports, words came after. For the child the paper calls Coral, the checklist noted she understood 97 words at 12 months, and her model had 91.

Across all eight children, the models and the children hit the same vocabulary milestones within an average of 22 days of each other, with the worst case 56 days.

The models also reproduced the differences between children, landing close to each child’s own halfway age.

In a recent development, they did not match perfectly. The models tended to start learning words a little late and then catch up faster, so the shape of the curve was only partly right.

The surprise in the paper is what happened when the researchers took replay away.

Sources indicate that coral’s household produced something like 10 million words a year, which is a rich environment by any measure. Hearing all of it once, in order, wasn’t enough. With a single pass the program barely learned words at all.

Around 25 to 30 passes over each day’s material was enough, and more than that added very little.

Industry observers note that the researchers link this to what sleep is thought to do for memory. A program replaying audio files is not a sleeping infant, and the paper is careful about that.

The amount of recording mattered just as much. Fed only a tenth of Coral’s daily speech, under an hour a day, the program learned none of the checklist words by 24 months.

At 30% of the day, about two and a half hours, it learned 80 of the 649 checklist words.

At 70% it got about nine-tenths of the way to the full result. The rarer words, it seems, only turn up for a listener who is there most of the day.

One limitation shapes everything else. Household recordings are full of clattering dishes, television, and two people talking at once, and the program was not asked to cope with any of that.

Instead the researchers transcribed all the speech around each child, then had a text-to-speech system read the transcripts back as clean audio.

Each household got a mix of eight adult female voices, with 30% of segments read in a voice matched to the child’s mother.

Sources indicate that so the word order, the timing and the vocabulary are real, and the sound isn’t. The acoustic problem a baby actually solves, picking one voice out of a noisy room, was left for later work.

Three of the eight children also had shorter recordings, 14 to 20 months of usable input, so their later trajectories are extrapolated rather than modeled.

The program also sees nothing: no faces, no pointing, no object being handed over, which is a large part of how toddlers work out what a word refers to.

The program learned sounds and words. It did not learn grammar, and whether the same machinery would arrive at sentence structure is the open question the authors name.

Recent findings suggest that the team wants to use the setup for questions nobody can put to a real baby. What would less sleep do, or screen speech instead of a parent’s?

Future studies could also add eye contact and the rest of the social world the cameras captured but the model never saw.

Hadas Raviv, a computational cognitive scientist in Princeton’s psychology department who built the analysis pipeline, framed the goal as the opposite of the usual one in artificial intelligence.

“Unlike much of modern AI, which aims for superhuman performance, we’re trying to understand how humans learn and how that learning gives rise to intelligence,” Raviv mentioned.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

Sources indicate that sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., left, has revealed a challenge to current Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

It has been revealed that sen. Chris Van Hollen announced Thursday night that he would run for Senate majority leader, launching a challenge to Sen. Charles E. Schumer of Latest York, the current Democratic leader.

According to recent reports, van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat first elected to the Senate in 2016, served in leadership in the House and has been chairman of both the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. He has said since the midterm elections he was listening to fellow Senate Democrats about the possibility of a run for the top job.

Industry observers note that “In this election, the American people called for change. They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people,” Van Hollen mentioned in a statement. “It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need latest leadership. This is not about any one person – it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”.

Schumer has already said he has the votes needed to continue serving as the leader.

According to recent reports, “I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the vital work ahead. I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader. I look forward to leading our latest Democratic majority and delivering for the American people,” Schumer stated in a statement.

According to recent reports, schumer's supporters were quick to highlight the success at the ballot box in 2026, with the Democratic caucus potentially growing to 56 seats if former Rep. Mary Peltola prevails in Alaska.

“Chuck has outlined an aggressive initiative for the new Democratic majority which is directly responsive to the message we heard from the voters, and he has the experience and unique mastery of the Senate process to make it happen,” Sen. Angus King, a Maine independent who caucuses with the Democrats, said in a statement. “Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?”.

According to recent reports, in keeping with the World Series theme, Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., echoed King with her own statement of support for Schumer.

It has been revealed that “The Brewers just had a record season, and next year is not the time to change our management," Baldwin said. "The same is true in the Senate.”.

In an interview with MS NOW about his run, Van Hollen conceded that Schumer would be the favorite in the secret-ballot contest, which will take place in December.

“Am I the underdog? Yes,” Van Hollen remarked. “You’re talking about an incumbent who uses the power of incumbency to, you know, provide deals to people.”.

Van Hollen outlined legislative priorities including restoring Medicaid funding that Republicans cut in last year's budget reconciliation law and extending Affordable Care Act tax credits. But he suggested Democrats need to go further.

"We need to extend tax credits for the Affordable Care Act, but we can’t stop there, right? We have a completely broken health care system. It’s become profits, not people. And so my view is, we also need in the first 100 days to make health care more affordable for tens of millions of people," Van Hollen mentioned. "We need to immediately make it clear that nobody’s going to pay one penny to subsidize data centers. ... We need to make sure that we have a livable minimum wage.".

He also said he would not take sides in contested Democratic primaries, and he would make sure the DSCC did not take money from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC.

Recent findings suggest that van Hollen's early backers include progressive Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who emerged from a hotly contested Democratic primary in Michigan while the Senate Democratic political apparatus was backing Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich.

“In April, I was the first candidate in the country to call on Senator Chris Van Hollen to lead Senate Democrats, and I am proud to stand with him in his bid to become Senate Majority Leader,” El-Sayed remarked in a statement. “Michiganders demand money out of politics, money in pockets, and Medicare for All. Sen. Chris Van Hollen offers both the courage to go toe-to-toe with the Trump administration to deliver for working people and the experience to maneuver the Senate caucus. It’s why he has my full support to lead our caucus.”.

Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#42823. Breaking: Common fiber supplement eased knee arthritis pain and improved grip strength in six weeks

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (906 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Common fiber supplement eased knee arthritis pain and improved grip strength in six weeks

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (906 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A six-week trial found that inulin fiber supplements modestly reduced knee osteoarthritis pain and improved grip strength in some adults.
  • Adults with knee osteoarthritis who took inulin, a fiber found in chicory root, ended a six-week trial with less knee pain than volunteers on a placebo.
  • In a recent development, volunteers who took inulin alone also gained grip strength, a moderate effect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A six-week trial found that inulin fiber supplements modestly reduced knee osteoarthritis pain and improved grip strength in some adults.

Adults with knee osteoarthritis who took inulin, a fiber found in chicory root, ended a six-week trial with less knee pain than volunteers on a placebo. On a scale from zero to ten, their scores fell 1.11 points more.

In a recent development, volunteers who took inulin alone also gained grip strength, a moderate effect. Those who followed a digital exercise program, or combined both treatments, did not.

The work was led by the University of Nottingham in England, and its results appeared in February 2026.

In 2019, about 528 million people worldwide were living with osteoarthritis, according to the World Health Organization. The knee is the joint most often affected, with 365 million cases.

About 33 million U.S. adults have the condition, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates. Physical exercise may help relieve pain and improve function, the agency notes.

In the U.K., 5.4 million people have knee osteoarthritis, according to a 2025 report from the charity Arthritis UK.

“Our recent lived experience survey demonstrated that six in ten people are living in pain most or all of the time due to their arthritis,” said Professor Lucy Donaldson, the charity’s director of research.

Under its former name, Versus Arthritis, the charity was one of the trial’s funders.

Between May 2022 and February 2025, the researchers randomly assigned 136 adults to four groups, and 117 completed all assessments.

Those who finished averaged 67.5 years of age, and 58.1 percent were women.

One group took 0.7 ounces (20 grams) of inulin powder a day. A second followed Joint Academy, a digital physical therapy program that began with a call to a personal physical therapist.

A third group combined both, and a fourth took maltodextrin, a starch-based powder, as a placebo. For ethical reasons linked to blood sugar, the placebo dose was half the inulin dose.

Industry observers note that volunteers did not know whether they were taking inulin or the placebo, but those assigned to exercise knew it. The staff who measured outcomes were blinded to all treatments.

Inulin’s pain result only just reached statistical significance, with a 95 percent confidence interval spanning 0.04 to 2.18 points.

It has been revealed that exercise lowered pain scores by 1.55 points compared with placebo, and the combination by 1.67 points. No added benefit from combining the two emerged, though the sample was too small to reliably detect one.

On average, both single treatments exceeded the one-point drop that patients typically notice as meaningful. Exercise came close to the two-point threshold for feeling “much better.”.

A third of placebo takers also improved by at least one point, but only 11 percent improved by two points or more.

Sources indicate that inulin made people less sensitive to pressure and to repeated painful stimuli, two measures linked to how the nervous system processes pain. Exercise alone had no such effect.

“This study raises the exciting possibility that a simple dietary change – adding a fibre supplement to your breakfast or yogurt – could meaningfully reduce pain and improve physical function,” said Dr. Afroditi Kouraki of the University of Nottingham’s School of Medicine, the lead author.

In a recent development, exercise improved a timed up-and-go test and a 30-second chair-stand test. Inulin alone had no effect on either.

Inulin feeds gut bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids. Only inulin raised blood levels of butyrate, one of those fatty acids, and of GLP-1, a hormone made in the gut.

According to recent reports, within the inulin groups, higher GLP-1 was associated with better grip strength, in an exploratory analysis that needs independent replication. The authors offer no explanation for the combined group’s grip result.

“The link we observed between GLP-1 and grip strength is particularly intriguing and points to a broader gut-muscle-pain axis that warrants further investigation,” remarked Professor Ana Valdes, the senior author, also of the School of Medicine.

In a recent development, A 2024 Canadian trial of a similar fiber in adults with knee osteoarthritis and obesity reported gains in grip strength and mobility after six months. Its effect on knee pain was only a trend.

It has been revealed that the short duration may not capture the full effects of exercise, the researchers acknowledged. Expectation effects in the exercise groups cannot be ruled out either.

It has been revealed that dropout reached 21 percent in the two exercise groups, compared with 3.6 percent in the two groups without exercise. To compensate, allocation odds were shifted toward exercise during later recruitment, which may have introduced bias.

A second analysis that included dropouts, with missing scores statistically imputed, gave consistent results. Only the effect of exercise on the up-and-go test lost statistical significance.

Of 50 inulin takers who finished, 23 reported minor digestive effects such as wind and bloating. None stopped the supplement or dropped out because of them.

According to recent reports, U.K. government guidelines cited by the National Health Service call for 1.1 ounces (30 grams) of fiber a day, so the inulin dose alone supplied two-thirds of that.

Valdes sits on the scientific advisory boards of the nutrition manufacturer Chuckling Goat and of OLIPOP, roles declared unrelated to this study.

The study was published in the journal Nutrients.

#42821. The next ice age may have begun 2,000 years ago, but humans cut it short

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1235 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

The next ice age may have begun 2,000 years ago, but humans cut it short

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1235 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Buried plants on Baffin Island reveal when a remnant of the Laurentide Ice Sheet began growing again and how human-caused warming reversed its advance.
  • About 2,000 years ago, the last remnant of the ice sheet that once covered much of Canada began growing again on Baffin Island.
  • It expanded in bursts, then began retreating around 1960 as warmer summers melted more ice than winters added.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buried plants on Baffin Island reveal when a remnant of the Laurentide Ice Sheet began growing again and how human-caused warming reversed its advance.

About 2,000 years ago, the last remnant of the ice sheet that once covered much of Canada began growing again on Baffin Island.

It expanded in bursts, then began retreating around 1960 as warmer summers melted more ice than winters added.

The researchers argue that the regrowth marked the earliest stage of a new glaciation in North America, and that human-caused warming cut it short.

At the peak of the last glacial period, the Laurentide Ice Sheet covered much of Canada and reached into the northern United States.

“People always say that it disappeared, but that’s not true,” mentioned Nicolás Young, a geochemist at Columbia University’s Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory who led the study.

What’s left of it is the Barnes Ice Cap, on the central plateau of Baffin Island in Nunavut. Its bedrock is low for the Canadian Arctic, only about 1,640 feet (500 meters) above sea level.

The ice has lasted this long because it is roughly 2,300 feet (700 meters) thick, enough to lift its surface to where snow survives the summer.

In a recent development, young’s team wanted to know whether the ice cap had ever been smaller than it is today and then grown back. Gifford Miller of the University of Colorado Boulder was among the co-authors.

The answer matters beyond one ice cap, because models say glaciations over North America most likely begin on Baffin Island.

It has been revealed that the Barnes Ice Cap is frozen to the rock beneath it, so it doesn’t slide the way most glaciers do. Instead of grinding the ground as it spreads, it buries whatever is growing there and preserves it.

When the margin retreats, the moss and small plants it killed centuries ago come out of the ice.

Radiocarbon dating estimates when the plants died, giving researchers a way to date the ice’s advance.

In a recent development, young’s team collected 88 of those plants at or near the 2022 ice edge. About 70% of them died around the year 1800, give or take 200 years. Those were the coldest summers of the Little Ice Age.

Sources indicate that sixteen more came from a half-mile (800-meter) line running out from the ice edge. A drained lake there had let the margin retreat farther than anywhere else.

In an interview with Earth.com, Young said that result surprised the team.

The researchers hadn’t expected the ice cap to have been smaller than it is now at any point in the last several thousand years.

“This unique finding allowed us to unexpectedly use these plants to track the ice cap’s renewed expansion,” Young noted.

It has been revealed that the researchers also dated 35 boulders and bedrock surfaces around the ice cap. Rock that is open to the sky builds up a rare form of beryllium at a known rate.

The amount in a surface tells how long it has been uncovered.

All of the surfaces gave the same answer: the old ice sheet had retreated inside its 2022 position about 3,600 years ago.

The oldest plants along the half-mile line died around the year 1000, so the ice was already advancing by then.

Sources indicate that to fill the gap, the team turned to 186 radiocarbon dates from plants under smaller ice caps on the same plateau. Not one of those dates is older than the Common Era.

The authors read that as the moment, roughly 2,000 years ago, when the summer snowline dropped onto the plateau and ice began to build up across it.

So the Laurentide reached its smallest size between about 3,000 and 2,000 years ago and then started to grow. The authors count that reversal as the start of the next glaciation.

The ice advanced in pulses during cold spells and was nearing its largest modern extent by about 1800.

In a recent development, by 1960 the growth had stopped. Aerial photographs show the margin retreating from about 1961, and the ice cap has since given up between 650 and 2,600 feet (200 and 800 meters) of ground.

Snow also survives the summer on less and less of it.

Around 1960, about 35% of its surface was high enough for snow to last through the summer. By the early 2000s only 3% was, and since 2010 none of it has been.

There is no longer any part of the ice cap where snow can pile up and turn into ice.

Summer temperatures have been climbing since the late 1700s, and since the early 1960s warmer summers account for almost all of the ice cap’s losses. Those summers track the greenhouse gases people have added to the air.

Between 1750 and 1850, the total rose by only about 12 parts per million of carbon dioxide equivalent. By 1960 it had risen another 50, and by 2024 another 138.

“The expansion and retreat of ice sheets has been one of Earth’s most consistent patterns over the last 2.6 million years,” Young told Earth.com.

About 2,000 years ago, he said, the Laurentide was starting its next phase of expansion, as it should have. Then greenhouse gases ended that expansion in the middle of the 20th century.

In the 1970s, some climate scientists argued that a fresh ice age was coming, and the idea got a famous airing in Newsweek.

Young stated those scientists were essentially correct, even if the media twisted the story. “We did just barely start the next glaciation, but they didn’t know it at the time,” he said.

Behind that growth was a slow decline in summer sunlight at high northern latitudes, the orbital rhythm that paces ice ages.

It has been revealed that greenhouse gases did rise over those thousands of years, by about 20 parts per million. The authors found that was too small to overcome the cooling.

Sources indicate that computer models suggest the next glaciation will not begin for thousands of years. But those models usually define its start as the point where latest ice sheets hold enough ice to lower the sea by about 10 feet (3 meters) or more.

Young’s team said that would miss the earlier stage of ice growth that his team considers the start of a glaciation.

Recent findings suggest that A 2025 study built from ocean sediments and Earth’s orbit estimated that the first regrowth of ice in this interglacial would come somewhere in the last 1,800 years or so. The plants on Baffin Island agree.

Sources indicate that what the record can’t yet say is exactly when the regrowth began. The plants that would date it are still under the ice, and only continued retreat will bring them out.

The dates so far are archived at the NSF Arctic Data Center.

Young said models of the ice cap’s future have it disappearing completely within the next few hundred years.

Asked what happens once the last piece of the Laurentide is gone, Young mentioned another glaciation is unlikely anytime soon.

“Given the amount of greenhouse gases that are in the atmosphere and that we continue to pump, the next glaciation is a long way off,” he noted.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#42819. Eleven pregnant garter snakes went to a San Francisco zoo, and now 62 of their young are in the wild

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1223 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Eleven pregnant garter snakes went to a San Francisco zoo, and now 62 of their young are in the wild

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1223 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 62 endangered San Francisco garter snakes born at the San Francisco Zoo were released in San Mateo County this fall, the first head-start release.
  • Geological Survey biologists caught 11 pregnant San Francisco garter snakes on the San Mateo County coast, in a preserve run by the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District (Midpen).
  • They took them to the San Francisco Zoo, where the snakes gave birth later that year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

62 endangered San Francisco garter snakes born at the San Francisco Zoo were released in San Mateo County this fall, the first head-start release.

In spring 2025, U.S. Geological Survey biologists caught 11 pregnant San Francisco garter snakes on the San Mateo County coast, in a preserve run by the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District (Midpen).

They took them to the San Francisco Zoo, where the snakes gave birth later that year.

It has been revealed that after giving birth, the mothers were returned to the wild, the zoo says. The zoo’s team raised their young until they were major enough to be released.

On November 10, 2026, the San Francisco Zoo & Gardens remarked 62 of those zoo-born garter snakes had been released this fall in San Mateo County.

It was the first release under a head-starting program for the endangered subspecies. The announcement does not say how many are still alive.

Industry observers note that the San Francisco garter snake (Thamnophis sirtalis tetrataenia) is a subspecies of the common garter snake. The zoo says it lives only in San Mateo County and a small corner of Santa Cruz County.

Recent findings suggest that the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service describes red on the top of the head, a greenish-blue or blue belly, a wide pale stripe down the back and red and black stripes on the sides.

A major loss of habitat came after World War II. In the 1940s, the sag ponds along Skyline Boulevard, small ponds in low spots along a fault line, held hundreds of the snakes.

By the 1960s, nearly all of those ponds had been drained and built over, according to the Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy.

The snake went onto the first federal endangered species list on March 11, 1967, six years before the Endangered Species Act of 1973. The zoo estimates that a couple thousand remain in the wild today.

Federal biologists blame illegal collection, construction, drought and saltwater in coastal ponds. Bullfrogs and largemouth bass are on the list too, because they eat the snakes and their prey.

That prey includes threatened California red-legged frogs, which the snakes rely on for food, the zoo states.

Since 2004, the conservancy and the National Park Service have restored and enhanced 33 acres (13 hectares) of wetland, grassland and coastal scrub for the snakes, according to Midpen’s 2025 release. The work added fresh ponds for breeding habitat.

Garter snakes give birth to live young instead of laying eggs. In this subspecies, birth comes in July or August. A litter can hold 6 to 35 babies, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service species profile states.

After the 11 females arrived, the team scanned them with ultrasound. The early scans revealed that a goal of 80 to 120 live babies was feasible, Midpen reported in September 2025.

Later that month, the district estimated that the zoo’s Conservation Team was raising about 120 newborns.

Industry observers note that the zoo had practice with the species. Its staff bred San Francisco garter snakes in the 1990s to work out how to keep them.

From 2005, they developed care protocols with the San Diego Zoo on housing, diet, growth tracking and parasite checks, Midpen noted in 2025.

Rochelle Stiles, the zoo’s director of field conservation, described the goal of the zoo’s snake rearing work.

“By providing these young snakes with a safe environment during their most vulnerable stage of life, we’re giving them a stronger start in the wild,” she noted.

Sources indicate that head-starting works that way. The young are fed and sheltered until they are significant enough to handle predators and competition for food, a method that also saved an endangered wallaby population in Australia.

Each snake born at the zoo had a genetic test before it left, and the results set its destination. About one-third went back to the area where its mother had been caught.

In a recent development, the rest went to several other populations that were short on both snakes and genetic variety. Isolated groups slowly lose diversity, the same problem behind a proposed genetic rescue for Lassen red foxes in northern California.

Industry observers note that disease data mattered too. Laura Patterson coordinates amphibian and reptile conservation statewide for the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW).

She said a CDFW survey for snake fungal disease, an emerging disease found in many wild snakes, “aided in the selection process.”.

Industry observers note that the partners will not name the release sites. The zoo said secrecy protects the snakes from collectors, cars and disease.

Midpen biologist Karine Tokatlian also commented on the release. “Seeing these young snakes returning to the wild represents years of research, collaboration, habitat restoration and careful conservation work,” she said.

Removal from the endangered list requires at least 10 viable, self-sustaining breeding populations. Each one needs at least 200 snakes.

In a recent development, U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) ecologists had already tested the idea on a computer. In a 2023 paper in PLOS ONE, a team led by Jonathan Rose of the USGS Western Ecological Research Center simulated newly introduced populations started with newborns, juveniles, adults or a mix.

Sources indicate that head-started juveniles gave those populations the best chance of lasting. Releases would have to continue for at least 15 years to keep the risk of near-extinction low, the model mentioned.

According to recent reports, raising juveniles also takes fewer adults away from the donor site. Justin Sloan, acting deputy field supervisor at the USFWS Sacramento office, credited research, genetic testing, habitat work and specialized care.

Ariel Starr, a Midpen wildlife ecologist, looked beyond this one subspecies.

“The success of this project and the associated research will not only benefit the San Francisco garter snake but will also hopefully inform the recovery of many imperiled reptile species,” she said.

Sources indicate that the November announcement gives no survival rate for the 62. It also does not say how long they had been out when it was posted.

Industry observers note that survival is low even for snakes born in the wild. One study found only 2 percent of females born live to age 5, according to the USFWS.

According to recent reports, there is also a gap between the 2025 estimate of about 120 newborns and the 62 released. The zoo did not explain it.

Recent findings suggest that the 2023 model focused on snake demography. Its authors wrote that the genetics of the donor, captive and released snakes would also be a major concern for any reintroduction initiative.

In a recent development, more than 130 garter snakes were born at the zoo in 2026. They are being raised for a second round of releases in 2027. Monitoring of both rounds will show whether the populations at the sites grow.

Rachel Townsend, a National Park Service wildlife biologist, put the first round in proportion. “Releasing these snakes is a significant moment, but it is one step of many in a much larger recovery effort,” she remarked.

The mothers are back in the wild. This fall, 62 of their young were let go at sites the partners will not name.

The information was obtained from the San Francisco Zoo & Gardens.

Grand Canyon hotels reopen 81 days after a deadly flood, echoing a 1966 disaster

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grand Canyon's South Rim hotels reopen November 20 after an August flash flood cut off their water.
  • For the first time since the end of August, visitors can book a hotel room on the South Rim of the Grand Canyon again.
  • On Friday, November 20, the South Rim’s hotels reopened to overnight guests, including El Tovar, which has stood on the edge of the canyon since 1905.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Canyon's South Rim hotels reopen November 20 after an August flash flood cut off their water. In 1966, a flood wrecked 40% of the same pipeline project.

For the first time since the end of August, visitors can book a hotel room on the South Rim of the Grand Canyon again.

On Friday, November 20, the South Rim’s hotels reopened to overnight guests, including El Tovar, which has stood on the edge of the canyon since 1905.

In a recent development, they had been closed for 81 days. A flash flood on August 29 tore through Bright Angel Canyon, killed two hikers and badly damaged the pipeline that carries water to the South Rim.

It was not the first time. In 1966, while that same pipeline was being built, a flood destroyed or carried off about 40% of the project, according to the National Park Service.

The park announced on November 18 that six South Rim lodges would reopen on November 20: El Tovar Hotel, Thunderbird Lodge, Kachina Lodge, Bright Angel Lodge and Maswik Lodge, along with Yavapai Lodge, which is operated by Delaware North.

On the same day, the park moved from Stage 4 to Stage 3 water conservation measures, which it called an vital milestone in the restoration of South Rim water services.

Food and drink services will resume gradually, and the park is asking visitors to check its website for dining hours.

Conserving water is still vital. Guests, visitors and residents are asked to take shorter showers, turn off faucets when they are not in use and avoid unnecessary water use.

According to recent reports, the flash flood hit Bright Angel Canyon and the Phantom Ranch area at about 2:30 p.m. on August 29. By the next morning, 62 people had been evacuated from Phantom Ranch and the lower North Kaibab Trail.

Nearly all of the footbridges over Bright Angel Creek were destroyed.

It has been revealed that metal structures and debris washed into the Colorado River, which was closed to river traffic. In steep terrain, heavy rain can trigger flash floods in mountain rivers faster than expected.

Two hikers from Granbury, Texas, John Giusti, 46, and Brent Rosenkranz, 42, died in the flood.

A member of their hiking group was reported missing, and the park mentioned in its September 8 update that one person remained unaccounted for.

The flood badly damaged the Transcanyon Waterline, a 12½-mile pipeline built in the 1960s.

It carries water from Roaring Springs, on the North Rim side, down through the canyon and up to the South Rim, where it supplies drinking water and fire protection for every facility, including more than 800 historic buildings.

The park’s drinking water comes from a single spring connected to more than 6 miles of caves.

About 40% of the old pipeline between the Phantom Ranch area and the North Rim was damaged, and the water intakes at Bright Angel Creek and Roaring Springs were hit hard.

On August 31, the park stopped all overnight stays at its hotels, including Phantom Ranch, and the South Rim began living on stored water.

Sources indicate that the park stayed open for day visits. When it confirmed the closure, it noted South Rim food and drink services, the Grand Canyon Clinic and the post office would remain open, some with reduced hours, while campers could only dry camp.

On September 16, a second flash flood damaged a temporary water intake that crews were building at Bright Angel Creek.

No one was hurt, but crews had to work out what repairs were needed and how the damage would affect the timeline.

On September 19, the park mentioned it expected to start pumping water from the creek to a new treatment plant by November 16, and it was working on an agreement to haul about 200,000 gallons of water a day to keep its tanks from running low.

At the time, the South Rim was using about 137,000 gallons a day.

By November 18, the park remarked water services to the South Rim were being restored, which allowed the hotels to reopen two days later.

Sources indicate that the pipeline itself was born out of a water problem. From 1901 to 1932, the Santa Fe railroad brought drinking water to the South Rim by train every day, and the trains came back as needed until the late 1960s.

In the summer of 1961, a water train of 20 cars carried about 204,000 gallons.

In a recent development, construction of the Transcanyon Waterline began in January 1965, using 6-inch and 8-inch aluminum pipe. Most of the equipment was designed specifically for the project, and the rest of the work was done by hand.

A year later, the project was nearly finished when what the park calls a 1,000-year flood struck.

Fifteen inches of rain fell on the inner canyon, and the water carried away trees, boulders and sections of fresh pipe.

A survey after the flood found that about 40% of the project was destroyed or missing. The cost rose from $2 million to $5 million, and construction resumed in late 1967.

The flood’s high-water mark is still recorded on the walls of the Phantom Ranch Ranger Station.

It has been revealed that the old line was built to last about 30 years and has been in service for more than 50. Since 2010, it has suffered over 85 major breaks.

A single repair often costs more than $25,000, and crews can reach the inner canyon only by trail or helicopter.

Sources indicate that breaks had closed the hotels before. In December 2025, after three significant breaks since late October, the park suspended overnight stays on December 6 and reopened the lodges on December 17.

In 2023, the park began a $208 million project to replace the pipeline and modernize the water system.

The fresh pipeline on the south side of the canyon was not damaged by either flood this year, and before August 29 the park was just over a month away from starting to use it.

Some inner canyon trails reopened in late October, including the South Kaibab Trail below the Tipoff and the River Trail.

But the Black Bridge, the Silver Bridge, Phantom Ranch and the entire North Kaibab Trail remained closed, and the park warned that water would stay off at Mile-and-a-Half and Three-Mile Resthouses and at Havasupai Gardens for the rest of the winter.

Hikers must carry all their water and a way to filter or treat it.

Sources indicate that el Tovar, a National Historic Landmark since 1987, was built from local limestone and Oregon pine for nearly $250,000. The hotel, which has 78 rooms, is once again taking guests.

The park says water conservation remains important as operations resume, and that the patience of residents, visitors and businesses during the emergency helped it keep essential services running.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service’s releases on the reopening of South Rim lodging, the August 29 flash flood, the recovery blueprint, the projected water dates, the August 31 hotel closure, the two hikers who died, the second flash flood, the trail reopenings and the December 2025 hotel reopening, its pages on the Transcanyon Waterline and its history, and its page on El Tovar Hotel.

A brain region known for listening helps us speak

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • WASHINGTON — A part of the brain famous for listening is key for talking, too.
  • Industry observers note that data collected from people as they listen and try to talk show that this brain region, a small spot inside a larger area called Wernicke’s area, has a more expansive job than researchers thought when it comes to communicating.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

WASHINGTON — A part of the brain famous for listening is key for talking, too.

Industry observers note that data collected from people as they listen and try to talk show that this brain region, a small spot inside a larger area called Wernicke’s area, has a more expansive job than researchers thought when it comes to communicating. The results may help efforts to restore people’s voices. The results presented November 15 at the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience and published November 19 in Science.The study provides convincing evidence that this brain spot is critical for speech production, notes neurologist and language researcher Jeffrey Binder of the Medical College of Wisconsin in Milwaukee. “My hope is that this study will help scientists and clinicians accept a more accurate interpretation of this focal area” as an early stop on the pathway to saying a word.

It has been revealed that A small part of the brain, just above the left ear, was first described in 1874 by a neurologist Carl Wernicke as necessary for making sense of speech. People with damage there had trouble comprehending words. But some people also had trouble producing them. “Sounds were swapped, words were replaced with near misses,” Edward Chang of the University of California, San Francisco, said in a news briefing. “The basic question has been, ‘Why would damage to a hearing area of the brain break the ability to speak?’ That question has been open for 150 years.”The new research offers an answer: A small bit of Wernicke’s area (to be extremely specific, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus or lpSTG ) becomes active just before a word is spoken. “Every word that you have said today began in that small part above your left ear about a quarter of a second before you said it,” Chang said.

The finding adds to growing evidence that brain areas are more complex than people have appreciated, says neuroscientist Leigh Hochberg at Brown University in Providence, R.I. “I believe that one of the things we are going to learn over the next five, 10 years of this research, is that each part of the brain that, we were taught as a med student or a grad student, does this, probably does that and a whole lot more.”.

Recent findings suggest that scientists measured brain activity in 28 people before they had surgery for epilepsy or tumors. They were able to see that this brain region kicked on as a person listened to words, and also just before they attempted to speak. Cells there had preferences for certain sorts of words, long ones, for instance. “It’s more active when you’re about to say the word caterpillar than when you’re about to say the word cat,” mentioned Matthew Leonard, a cognitive neuroscientist at UCSF.

Electrical stimulation to this small bit of brain also interfered with people’s ability to talk. “What we found was that stimulation, really only in this lpSTG area, disrupted this speech production when it was delivered just prior to speaking,” said UCSF bioengineer Alexander Silva.

Some efforts to make implanted devices that can help restore speech to people who no longer talk focus on the motor cortex, a part of the brain that controls the movements required for speech. This bit of Wernicke’s area offers an additional spot to consider, Silva stated. “What if you could target a single brain region and gain access to the full spectrum of speech, from listening all the way up to speech production?”.

Experimental brain implants in two volunteers with paralysis were able to detect both what they heard and what they were trying to say, the researchers report in the study.

The discovery may help scientists better understand situations that involve both hearing and speaking, such as speech or comprehension differences in people with autism, or how children first begin learning to talk, Chang mentioned.

#42816. Meerkats cross the desert together, but what happens when one finds itself alone?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1270 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Meerkats cross the desert together, but what happens when one finds itself alone?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1270 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers tracked 20 meerkats in the Kalahari Desert to see how they navigated familiar territory after being separated from their groups.
  • According to recent reports, meerkats leave their burrows together each morning and forage as a group.
  • In South Africa’s Kalahari Desert, researchers carried 20 adult meerkats up to 0.9 miles from where they caught them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers tracked 20 meerkats in the Kalahari Desert to see how they navigated familiar territory after being separated from their groups.

According to recent reports, meerkats leave their burrows together each morning and forage as a group. How well can one find its way alone?

In South Africa’s Kalahari Desert, researchers carried 20 adult meerkats up to 0.9 miles from where they caught them.

In a recent development, after release, 18 reached a familiar spot or found their group. Fourteen headed first to the burrow where the group had slept.

The team found no clear advantage for older or more experienced animals.

The researchers suggest that daily group travel may give meerkats enough experience to navigate alone.

According to recent reports, the study was led by Mathilde Martin of the University of Zurich. The team worked alongside the Kalahari Meerkat Project, which follows about 15 wild groups accustomed to people.

The project is run from the Kalahari Research Centre, which is known as the KRC.

“At the KRC, our work with meerkats allows us to distract them with a water bottle and fit their collar in a few seconds while they stand upright drinking; a mere formality for them,” Martin said.

It has been revealed that A GPS tag on each collar logged the position of the animal once every second. A radio transmitter was also fitted, along with a small audio recorder for the meerkat’s calls.

The team tested a total of 20 adults from five groups between January and March 2025. Fifteen of these animals were male, whereas only five of them were female.

Each meerkat was caught while its group was foraging and was released up to 0.9 miles (1.5 kilometers) away.

Such a distance is greater than the ground usually covered by a meerkat group in a whole day.

The release sites were located inside the territory of each group. The team chose areas that the group had not visited for at least 30 days.

Recent findings suggest that homing experiments of this kind have previously been carried out on honeybees and desert ants. Highly social animals that travel in tight groups have rarely been tested in the same way.

This is because the knowledge of one animal is difficult to separate from the decisions of the group.

Eighteen of the 20 meerkats left the release site. The sleeping burrow, the capture spot or the group itself was reached by all 18 of them.

Some of the meerkats departed almost at once, whereas others circled the release site for nearly 90 minutes.

The area covered by them ranged from half an acre to almost 17 acres (2,050 to 68,200 square meters).

A meerkat rarely strayed from its course once a direction had been chosen. Sixteen of the animals aimed for a fixed place.

The sleeping burrow was visited first by 14 of those 16.

On average, the straight-line distance to the target amounted to 82% of the distance actually walked by the meerkat.

The release areas had not been visited by the group for a month. The team therefore concluded that the meerkats had been navigating from long-term memory.

Two males never left the release site, and they were carried back to their groups after 90 minutes. They were no younger or less experienced than the others.

The authors suspect that stress kept them there, and not a lack of knowledge.

Recent findings suggest that some meerkats had been expected to navigate better than others. Subordinate males sometimes leave the group and go alone in search of mates.

Other females are occasionally driven out for a while by the dominant female.

Solo trips of this kind could be counted as practice. The researchers also considered the age of each animal, together with the time it spent on guard duty.

Attention was given as well to how often it scent-marked the territory or dug at shelters.

According to recent reports, none of those traits predicted how long a meerkat explored. Neither did they predict how accurately it set off or how straight it travelled.

No clear difference was found between males and females either, although only five females took part.

The authors think that the explanation lies in the territory itself. It is small and stable, with 0.3 to 0.6 miles (0.5 to 1 kilometer) covered by a group daily.

The whole territory has probably been crossed several times by each member by the time adulthood is reached.

The authors wrote that pigeons of different ages are likewise able to find their way home equally well.

On the way home, the meerkats spent about two-thirds of their time searching for cues. Most of the remaining time was spent moving.

Few of them stopped to eat, and those that did only grabbed millipedes crawling on the sand.

The animals stood upright or climbed a bush or tree trunk in order to scan the landscape. Overall, they spent 10 times longer on looking than on sniffing.

This balance between looking and sniffing was altered late in the trip. By that stage, a meerkat had reached its target and was searching for its group. Sniffing then took up more than 20% of its cue-searching time.

Recent findings suggest that along the way, meerkats were often seen sniffing around boltholes. These are the small shelters that the animals dig across their territory. An earlier experiment had found that meerkats remember where their boltholes are.

The authors suggested that boltholes may serve as landmarks in a meerkat’s memory of its territory.

The search was not ended by reaching the burrow, because the group could have moved on since the capture.

Industry observers note that thirteen of the 20 meerkats rejoined their groups on their own. The slowest took almost three hours.

Industry observers note that the burrow or the capture site was reached by five others. The group had nevertheless not been found by them when the three-hour limit ran out.

These animals were caught again and returned by the team.

It has been revealed that the researchers could not explain why some meerkats succeeded while others did not. Success was not predicted by a straighter trip to the burrow.

Nor was it predicted by the number of scent marks left behind by the group.

The tracking of a group was compared by the authors to a predator following its prey. The target keeps moving and its route is not known to the searcher.

Twenty animals make up a small sample, as the authors wrote. All of them were subordinate adults older than 10 months, so pups and dominant animals were not tested.

Every release was also made inside familiar territory. The results therefore do not show how a meerkat would manage in a place it does not know.

According to recent reports, two reasons for looking around could not be fully separated either. A lone meerkat that scans the landscape may be checking for predators as much as searching for landmarks.

If many group members know the territory, the next question is who leads when the group moves.

The authors want to know whether certain traits influence which animal takes the lead. The physical needs of an animal and its social rank are two examples.

Co-author Benjamin Robira said the team now wants to understand what makes up a meerkat’s mental picture of its territory.

The researchers also intend to study how the animals get from one point to another.

The full study was published in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

The 6 Best Electric Snow Shovels for Swiftly Clearing Sidewalks and Driveways
