Industry News: What satellites leave behind

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3260 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was the lithium that gave it away, claims Daniel Murphy, an atmospheric chemist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
  • It was early 2023, in Fairbanks, Alaska, in the deep blue of winter, and Murphy and his colleagues had just sent a plane through the stratosphere, the atmospheric stratum 6 to 31 miles (10 to 50 kilometers) above Earth’s surface where the protective ozone layer lies.
  • According to recent reports, their experiment came as interest was growing in controversial proposals to cool the planet by injecting certain aerosols into the atmosphere — a form of geoengineering.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was the lithium that gave it away, claims Daniel Murphy, an atmospheric chemist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

It was early 2023, in Fairbanks, Alaska, in the deep blue of winter, and Murphy and his colleagues had just sent a plane through the stratosphere, the atmospheric stratum 6 to 31 miles (10 to 50 kilometers) above Earth’s surface where the protective ozone layer lies.

According to recent reports, their experiment came as interest was growing in controversial proposals to cool the planet by injecting certain aerosols into the atmosphere — a form of geoengineering. The team hoped to get a baseline measurement of the chemistry of the upper atmosphere, before any geoengineering experiments altered the hard-to-reach atmospheric layer.

The lithium showed they were too late.

The team expected to find trace amounts of metals naturally deposited by meteoroids, which constantly bombard and burn up in Earth’s atmosphere. But their data indicated way more lithium in stratospheric particles than is typically present in meteoroids.

“That’s what led us to the other metals,” Murphy states. Analyzing their samples, they also found higher than expected levels of aluminum, plus significant amounts of other metals like copper and lead that are scarcely found in meteoroids and must have come from some other source. Then there were the more exotic metals like niobium and hafnium, which appeared in their samples in the same ratio as in an alloy used to manufacture rocket engine nozzles.

In a recent development, the data pointed to an obvious culprit: human-made objects such as satellites and spent rocket stages that fall back to Earth from orbit and reenter the atmosphere. On the way down, they wear away and disintegrate under the heat of friction — a process known as ablation.

Later that year in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), Murphy and his colleagues reported that 10% of stratospheric aerosol particles carried metals from spacecraft.

The number was shocking, but not altogether surprising. Reentries have been rising sharply in recent years as corporations and countries began launching megaconstellations of thousands of satellites, like SpaceX’s Starlink. And all those satellites will inevitably deorbit.

In a recent development, since Murphy and his colleagues’ 2023 report, it’s become clear that human-made satellites are now dumping more of certain metals into the upper atmosphere than meteoroids naturally do. This influx has raised concerns that the metals might catalyze chemical reactions that destroy ozone, alter cloud formation, or boost or buffer the greenhouse effect.

In a recent development, researchers say it’s too soon to know for sure if the metals are a serious environmental problem. But megaconstellations are growing faster than our ability to close these knowledge gaps.

Industry observers note that at the same time, the uncertainty over whether regulators might have to act presents a major risk to the space industry, states Martin Ross of the Aerospace Corporation, a research and development nonprofit based in El Segundo, California, and a co-author of the 2023 study. “We would call it an enterprise risk,” says Ross, “in that the longer we wait to see if there is something going on, the bigger the mitigation will be — if there needs to be any mitigation — down the line.”.

From our vantage point on Earth, space may be incomprehensibly vast, but the orbital environment is not.

Six years ago, according to the U.S. Space Force’s public catalog, there were some 13,700 trackable objects circling in low Earth orbit; last year, the number had climbed to nearly 25,000. Disposing of satellites in the atmosphere reduces overcrowding and the risk of uncontrolled objects crashing into each other — and potentially setting off a chain of collisions that wipe out key space-based technologies or turn Earth orbit into an impenetrable debris field.

RELATED: Our increasingly cluttered skies.

Sources indicate that “Reentry is the only sustainable, short-term way of cleaning up the orbital environment,” says José Pedro Ferreira, a doctoral candidate in astronautical engineering at the University of Southern California (USC) in Los Angeles, who left an industry job for academia in the early 2020s when it became clear that reentry could have unintended consequences. “We need to do it, otherwise we may undermine our capability of accessing orbit.”.

But operators are also typically held responsible by their national regulators for any damages their spacecraft cause on the ground, and for decades the industry has designed spacecraft to burn up as much as possible in the atmosphere to minimize the risk to lives and infrastructure on the ground, a principle known as design for demise.

As a result, the space industry has long perceived its impacts to Earth as minimal. But in the age of megaconstellations, that’s no longer the case.

“As with everything, we live in a closed system,” notes Ferreira, “and things do not disappear.”.

It has been revealed that spaceX released its first 60 satellites into orbit in May 2019 to bring internet to even remote regions of the globe; less than a decade later, Starlink’s constellation is more than 10,000 satellites strong. Starlink already comprises roughly two-thirds of active satellites, and SpaceX intends to grow it to as many as 42,000. Other countries and corporations are not far behind: Amazon Leo is authorized by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to operate roughly 7,700 satellites; China has plans to deploy some 28,000.

Not only are we launching more than ever, but we’re also bringing spacecraft back down faster than ever before.

Industry observers note that for decades, spacecraft have been designed to burn up as much as possible upon reentry to minimize risks to those on the ground. As a result, the space industry has long perceived its impacts to Earth as minimal. But in the age of megaconstellations, that’s no longer the case.

Industry observers note that historically, satellite operators had what Ferreira calls a “gentleman’s agreement” to deorbit their spacecraft within 25 years of mission termination to prevent orbital clutter. Recently, some national authorities have begun enforcing even tighter timelines. The FCC, for example, now enforces a five-year window.

“If you have 50,000 satellites in orbit, which is almost surely going to be reached in the not too distant future, with a design lifetime of five years,” Murphy says, “that would mean a satellite would be reentering and burning up in the atmosphere on average more than once an hour.”.

Recent findings suggest that operators of megaconstellations may use even shorter timelines for deorbiting satellites, according to Ferreira, bringing them down at the first sign of malfunction. “Which is great from a standpoint of orbital sustainability,” he notes, “but it starts raising the question more and more about what the impacts are in the atmosphere.”.

There are reasons to be concerned.

Sources indicate that aluminum, for example, which makes up the bulk of most spacecraft, may form aluminum oxides as it breaks down during ablation, which can kick-start a chain of chemical reactions that eat away at ozone, Earth’s main shield against UV radiation. Some atmospheric models suggest that metals from spacecraft in stratospheric particles could seed polar stratospheric clouds, further accelerating ozone depletion.

According to recent reports, injecting aluminum into the upper atmosphere is also the basis of many controversial geoengineering looks. Aluminum compounds would block radiation from the Sun, which could cool down our warming planet. But they might also entrap radiation reflected off the surface of the ocean, which could increase surface temperatures. Opposition to geoengineering has so far stymied any field experiments, but with the number of reentries rising from a few hundred to many thousands per year, an uncontrolled geoengineering experiment on a grand scale may have already begun.

It has been revealed that “The metals are at the same altitude range as the ozone layer, so we have to be concerned about what they would do,” Murphy notes. “We don’t know it’s bad, but we don’t know it isn’t bad either.”.

Industry observers note that one reason it’s so difficult to predict the impacts of ablation is that we don’t yet understand what happens to spacecraft during ablation. “We reenter things all the time and we have been since the moment we started launching spacecraft,” says Stijn Lemmens, a space debris mitigation analyst at the European Space Agency (ESA). “It’s fascinating, for something which is so ubiquitous, how little we actually know about it, and how little we used to care about it.”.

Operators have long been incentivized to design spacecraft to burn up as much as possible in the atmosphere, and decades of this design for demise ethos has given the space industry a solid idea of how much material — or how little — will make it to the ground when objects burn through the atmosphere.

But in terms of that material that is ablated, “we’re really in the dark,” says Ross. Previous studies have suggested that around 90% of the bodies of orbiting satellites and spent upper stages could be vaporized, later condensing into the nanosized particles the team detected. But, says Ross, “we really don’t understand how these vehicles melt, how they break apart, how they form smoke trails.”.

To quantify the impacts on the atmosphere, researchers start with atmospheric models and then add ablated material, examining how those particles interact with the natural stratospheric background via complex chemical reactions and physical processes like mixing. But the outputs of the atmospheric models are at the moment held back by our limited understanding of the fiery, complex process of ablation — details like what compounds are being emitted and what size particles are being formed. “We’re basically guessing at this point,” Ross says. “And we’re getting to the limit of what we can do with guessing.”.

Sources indicate that to do better, scientists are developing newly introduced models of the physics and chemistry of ablation itself. At USC, Ferreira and his colleagues model how ablation produces aluminum oxides in the upper atmosphere, providing atmospheric researchers with inputs for both emissions and particle size. In a 2024 study in Geophysical Research Letters, the team reported that a 550-pound (250 kilograms) satellite — about the size of your average megaconstellation satellite — could deposit some 66 pounds (30 kg) of aluminum oxide nanoparticles in the upper atmosphere. Such particles could remain aloft for upwards of 30 years, potentially catalyzing ozone-destroying reactions as they settle throughout the stratosphere for decades after reentry.

Sources indicate that but state-of-the-art ablation models don’t always agree on what products are being formed, according to Ross. A model from researchers at the University of Leeds in the U.K. suggests that aluminum hydroxide, rather than aluminum oxide, may be the main byproduct.

To validate ablation models and get more useful data from atmospheric models, we need more measurements from reentries. How an object breaks apart as it tumbles through the air is a messy process — a product of astrophysics, fluid mechanics, materials science, and engineering. “You cannot reproduce it on Earth,” Lemmens says. “There is no facility large enough to, in one assessment, combine all the effects.”.

That means scientists need to measure ablation where it’s actually taking place — “take instruments and put them on airplanes and go out and watch these things reenter,” Ross indicates.

Recent findings suggest that since the beginning of the Space Age, these kinds of measurements have only been taken a handful of times. Observing space objects from an airplane as they streak through the atmosphere is difficult work — and potentially dangerous. Most reentering objects are uncontrolled, making it hard to predict exactly where the object will hit the atmosphere and how much of it will burn up in the process. Researchers need a degree of certainty to avoid sending a plane full of scientists and sensors up into a debris field. “These types of reentries, which are destructive and still predictable so that you can get close, are extremely rare,” Lemmens indicates.

But in 2024, ESA got lucky. The first of four Cluster II satellites — released in 2000 to study Earth’s magnetosphere — was poised to reenter the atmosphere, and the agency had a pretty good idea of exactly where and when it would break up over the southern Pacific Ocean.

“We could get close,” Lemmens indicates. “The drawback is it was in broad daylight, which had not been attempted before on this level of detail.”.

In daytime, the team would have no visual confirmation of reentry, and it would be harder to get clean data than at night. The team had to trust they were pointing their instruments at the right spot, and then look at their data after the fact to see if they caught it. “In the end, it’s a leap of faith,” Lemmens says. “You predict as well as you can, you fly the plane as well as you can, but in the end, you do it all in the blind,” he says.

Industry observers note that on Sept. 8, a team of scientists took off from Easter Island on a modified Dassault Falcon 900 business jet packed with instruments, and pointed their cameras just above the bright blue horizon roughly 500 miles (800 km) away.

The team used spectroscopic instruments to identify which vapors were coming from the ablating satellite. Since the team knew the material makeup of the satellite, they could gauge its surface temperatures during reentry, as the appearance of specific ions would indicate a certain material had reached its melting point.

In a recent development, altogether, they captured about 20 seconds of the reentry. Two more satellites from the same cluster were set to reenter within 24 hours of each other on Aug. 31 and Sept. 1, 2026, giving ESA another opportunity to capture more of the reentry process and to fully reconstruct the breakup.

For researchers, one upside to the rapid and unmitigated increase in satellite reentries is more opportunities to capture the process in action.

Sources indicate that some of the best data yet to come will be collected by ESA’s Draco mission, in which the agency intends to build and launch a satellite with the “sole purpose of falling apart again,” claims Lemmens. Draco will launch in 2027 with an indestructible capsule that will survive reentry, protecting the data collected from the surface of the satellite as it’s torn apart by the atmosphere.

Recent findings suggest that researchers will be able to combine these onboard data with remote observations, using them to improve or validate existing models of ablation. “That means we, for the first time, will actually have the full story without any ambiguities,” Lemmens says.

Once a scientific consensus is reached, then mitigation measures, whether technological or regulatory, can be deployed.

If research confirms that one material or another in spacecraft is particularly damaging to the atmosphere, for example, space operators can remove and replace it. “That was the basis of the success of the Montreal Protocol,” says Ross.

It has been revealed that after scientists discovered a hole in the ozone layer in the 1980s, every country in the world signed on to the Montreal Protocol, an international agreement to control the ozone-depleting substances humans were emitting into the atmosphere. The hole has been shrinking ever since. Signed in 1987, the agreement is widely considered one of the most successful environmental treaties to date. Since then, however, other global climate agreements have not fared as well.

According to recent reports, still, many remain optimistic, including Ross. He points to the commercial space industry’s track record of working with regulators and astronomers to reduce space debris and light pollution. “There is some current flowing in those lines,” he claims.

RELATED: Can robots save Earth orbit?

Industry observers note that some operators have already expressed a commitment to acting on whatever guidelines come out of research on the atmospheric risks. “The difficulty that I have as a responsible operator is, in this particular case, I don’t know what to do,” Vijay Thakur, a technical authority at French satellite corporation Eutelsat, said at an October 2025 panel at the Secure World Foundation’s 7th Summit for Space Sustainability in Paris. There are clear brightness limits he can follow to mitigate impacts to the astronomical community, he noted, but no such guidelines exist yet for atmospheric impacts.

In a recent development, “I want to put the right technical requirements, for me as the operator customer, onto industry so they can build what I need to operate and take it up and bring it back down without damaging anything from 0 kilometers to the von Kármán line,” Thakur mentioned, referring to the commonly accepted boundary of outer space at 62 miles high (100 km). “Help.”.

There are some design tweaks at the moment available that could reduce emissions and help more of each spacecraft survive reentry, including non-ablative heat shields and inflatable aerodynamic decelerators, according to Adam Mitchell, a materials and processes evaluation engineer at ESA.

It has been revealed that of course, the more of a spacecraft that survives reentry, the greater the risk on the ground during uncontrolled reentries — and most reentries are uncontrolled. “There is this balance between sustainability and safety, but when it comes to human safety, there is no compromise at all,” Chris Young, space sustainability senior lead at the U.K. Space Agency, said at the same Secure World Foundation panel. “Design for demise has to take priority.”.

Recent findings suggest that satellite builders could also consider replacing problematic metals — but that comes with its own trade-offs. In 2024, the world’s first wooden satellite, LignoSat, launched to orbit in a partnership between Kyoto University and Japanese logging firm Sumitomo Forestry. A cube of magnolia wood panels, LignoSat will give researchers insights into how well wood holds up in the space environment, and how cleanly it burns up in the atmosphere. Carbon fiber is another material of interest, according to Ferreira. But these organic materials may release black carbon into the upper atmosphere, which may absorb sunlight or reflect it, depending on the structure the carbon takes.

Ross thinks we can close the remaining knowledge gaps in short order — and that those lessons can be applied almost immediately. “We can do that before the next generation of satellites comes along,” he states, “but we just need the resources.”.

A cultural revolution is coming for the industry, regardless of what’s discovered about the impacts to the atmosphere. “The one-use, nonrecyclable culture that we have in space, of, ‘We’ll launch something to space with rare Earth minerals that are of limited supply and then burn them all up in the atmosphere after one use,’ that is unsustainable,” stated Young.

It has been revealed that A sustainable future — one that balances both Earth and space sustainability — will involve creating something we haven’t quite nailed yet in our earthbound industries. “We need to move beyond the single-use mindset that currently defines much of spacecraft design and accelerate the transition toward an in-space circular economy,” Mitchell says.

Can we do in space what we’ve failed to do on Earth? Right now, researchers are gathering data as fast as they can, as fast as resourcing allows, to inform models of ablation and atmospheric processes that will eventually be validated by measurements taken during reentry.

Then, equipped with actionable data, we can act.

Bipartisan process for picking GAO chief breaks down

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (943 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept.
  • Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.
  • According to recent reports, sources said Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who presently serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept. 23. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.

According to recent reports, sources said Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who presently serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget. The White House submitted ethics paperwork on Ueland — required for nominations — to the GAO, according to a source.

Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., on Thursday posted notice of a committee hearing Nov. 19 to examine more than a dozen presidential nominees for executive and judicial offices, including “a nominee to be Comptroller General.”.

According to recent reports, the post identifies by name all of the nominees except the candidate for comptroller general. The post has been filled by an acting comptroller general, Orice Williams Brown, since Gene L. Dodaro completed his 15-year term at the end of last year.

The move by Paul to short-circuit the convening of a legislative commission to recommend candidates infuriated top Democrats, who excoriated the chairman in a joint statement Wednesday night. A special bipartisan, bicameral legislative commission is supposed to recommend at least three candidates for comptroller general to the president, according to statute.

It has been revealed that homeland Security Committee GOP staff solicited recommendations for a comptroller general from some Democratic congressional offices Wednesday afternoon, imposing a deadline of 8 a.m. Thursday, according to Democratic aides.

The president nominates the head of the GAO, the investigative arm of Congress, with the advice and consent of the Senate.

In a recent development, paul pushed back on the criticism Thursday, saying, “Democrats have known about this for months and months and months.” He remarked the last time the special commission made recommendations for the office, when Barack Obama was president, “Democrats submitted their own list, Republicans submitted their own list. So they can complain all they want but they just need to make their list and submit it.”.

In the past, however, the special commission convened, sought applications for the position, interviewed candidates and deliberated before sending recommendations to the president.

A 1980 law states that when there is a vacancy in the comptroller general position, “there is established a commission to recommend individuals to the President for appointment to the vacant office,” and that the commission must submit at least three names.

Under the statute, the commission includes the speaker, Senate majority and minority leaders, House majority and minority leaders, chairs and ranking members of the Senate Homeland Security and House Oversight and Government Reform committees, and the Senate president pro tempore.

Industry observers note that in 1981, for example, after the law took effect, the two congressional leaders, Speaker Thomas P. “Tip” O’Neill Jr., D-Mass., and Senate Majority Leader Howard H. Baker, R-Tenn., sent a letter to President Ronald Reagan saying the special commission had met and voted to recommend eight candidates to succeed Comptroller General Elmer Staats.

“The members of the Commission have taken their statutory responsibility seriously,” they wrote.

Reagan nominated Charles A. Bowsher, who was on the list, and he was confirmed.

After Bowsher’s term ended in 1996, the commission eventually formed, interviewed multiple candidates, and deliberated for several months. Republicans controlled both chambers, and Bill Clinton was president. The members of the commission could not reach agreement, and as a result, the Republicans on the committee submitted their list to Clinton, and the Democrats on the panel submitted theirs.

It has been revealed that clinton also had his own list. Clinton nominated David M. Walker, who was on all three lists, and he was confirmed by the Senate more than two years after Bowsher’s departure. Walker argued Thursday against short-circuiting the commission process.

Sources indicate that “The position is of critical importance and the related statutory Commission process should not be circumvented," Walker stated. "Doing so would undercut the credibility of the person and the effectiveness of the GAO.”.

Walker resigned in March of 2008, when George W. Bush was still president. He appointed Dodaro as acting comptroller general when he left. The commission got going several months later, creating a website with application instructions and candidate questions.

Recent findings suggest that over the next two years, the commission interviewed some 20 candidates. Democrats and Republicans on the panel were unable to reach agreement, and Democrats, who had a majority on the commission, submitted their own list to Obama in 2010. Republicans followed up with their list.

“The Commission has been working in earnest on this undertaking for more than one year and has dedicated considerable time and effort to present you with highly qualified candidates for this crucial position,” then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., along with other Democratic leaders, wrote to Obama when they submitted the Democrats’ list.

The Democrats’ move drew a rebuke from Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who was ranking member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee at the time.

Collins said in a statement she was “extremely disappointed” that Democrats “abruptly ended the selection process for the next Comptroller General without a bipartisan agreement” on the recommendations. “We have had several exceptionally qualified individuals apply to be the next leader of the GAO, and it should have been possible to come up with a consensus list.”.

Obama nominated and the Senate confirmed Dodaro, who was one of four recommendations from the Democrats.

Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

It’s one of the few backyard upgrades that actually changes how you use your space, whether you’re dealing with sore muscles, trying to carve out a little quiet at the end of the day, or just want a place to hang out that isn’t your couch.

If you still aren’t sure about whether or not you think it’s worth the purchase, know that there’s a crop of new hot tubs that can ship right to your door and don’t take too long to set up. You can get some simple plug-and-play models up and running in an afternoon, elevating your outdoor space from a simple yard to a true getaway spot. Others are closer to a full installation, though the trade-off is typically stronger jets, better insulation, and more built-in features. You also have options like basic inflatables, molded shells, or acrylic spas with lighting, waterfalls, and app controls.

For our recommendations, we focused on how these tubs are built, their lineups of features, and what you’re really getting for the price. Here are the ones worth considering, plus what to know before you commit to this major purchase.

To guide our selections, we leaned on our own experience owning hot tubs and spas, from basic models to custom setups.

Industry observers note that we chose hot tubs that range from just under $1,000 for inflatable models to high-end models that nearly mimic showroom-quality tubs. But all are available to buy online. Beyond price, we looked at features, capabilities, and fun extras like speakers and ice buckets. Some are a must, while others are mere perks that can elevate your time in the hot tub—and the price.

We pored over customer reviews and expert write-ups. We also consulted Jeff Courter, an engineer and former owner of Cache Valley Spas in Logan, Utah, to get his insights on how you should factor price, setup, and features into your decision.

In a crowded field of plug-and-play spa contenders, the AquaRest DayDream stands out for a long list of relaxing reasons. It’s a legit backyard spa without the headache of professional installation and electrical upgrades, which puts this spa in that sweet spot between bargain shopping and custom installs.

We like that it plugs into a standard outlet but still delivers a surprisingly strong massage thanks to 35 jets. AquaRest states the DayDream uses a Jacuzzi-branded pump—and while that doesn’t make it a Jacuzzi spa, it’s still a solid indicator you’re getting a reputable, name-brand component under the hood.

There are so many nice extras, like ozone filtration and a lighted waterfall, that make it feel more like a full spa setup than a starter tub. The trade-off is in the materials and power: The roto-molded shell isn’t as luxe as pricier acrylic models, and heating can be slow on 120 volts. There is the option to use a 240-volt setup, if you’ve got the capacity. Given the price and host of features, this hot tub is a great choice for those looking to make a long-term investment.

More: Best Inflatable Hot Tubs for Backyard Bliss.

If you’re looking for a solid hot tub without overspending, we like the Coleman SaluSpa line. The Sicily AirJet is a great choice within that line because it gives you a larger soaking area, 180 AirJets, and a 314-gallon water capacity without jumping into hard-sided spa pricing. This is still an inflatable model, so it does not have the same insulation, jet pressure, or long-term durability you get from a permanent acrylic spa, but the feature set is strong for the price.

Our family has been using a SaluSpa for several months now, and I find it easy to maintain as well. We especially like that the package includes the pump, cover, chemical floater, two filter cartridges and repair patch, which makes the first setup feel simple and straightforward.

According to recent reports, we have found the hot tub is hard to connect to the companion app, but we also have no problem controlling it from the panel and do not find a need for an app. For shoppers looking for a quality inflatable that won’t break the bank and has solid reviews, this is a roomy, feature-heavy pick that feels like a better value than many smaller inflatables.

Industry observers note that inflatable hot tubs are a great option for folks who want to relax at home without making a more permanent decision (and investment). If you’re looking for a roomy, tricked-out inflatable hot tub to enhance your wellness, the Intex PureSpa Greywood Deluxe checks quite a few boxes.

According to recent reports, with 170 bubble jets, a multifunction heater, filter, blower, and hard water treatment system, this model has more features than many inflatables. With a capacity of 290 gallons and included headrests, there is plenty of room for lounging. If you like the features of this tub, but have less space to work with, there is also a smaller four-person model available.

It has been revealed that we like that—for the price—this hot tub includes a lot of fun extras. In addition to the water treatment and jet specs, there’s also a multicolor LED light system and wireless touch button control panel. There are two headrests, a cover, ground tarp, and storage bag included as well.

According to recent reports, we do wish there were more than two headrests for a hot tub advertised for six people, but it’s not a deal breaker. One note: Check your available ground space before ordering, too, as this hot tub has a larger footprint than some other popular models.

This hot tub solves a lot of the problems folks face when seeking a therapeutic experience at home—they may not have the space or ability to upgrade the electrical system.

According to recent reports, the hard-sided LifeSmart plugs into a standard outlet, skips complicated installation, and still delivers a solid massage with 13 jets, all in a compact, patio-friendly footprint. If you’re hoping to place this hot tub on an elevated surface, though, it’s important to consult a professional and check the load your deck can bear.

In a recent development, even compact four-person models like this one can weigh over 3,000 pounds when filled with water, which is more than most standard decks can handle without added support. And while it’s listed as a four-seater, many consumers say it's comfiest with two to three adults.

Industry observers note that if aesthetics matter as much as performance, this Comfort hot tub leans into both. The acrylic shell and clean wood-look cabinet design give it a more built-in, high-end vibe than most entry-level spas (which typically have rotomolded, all-in-one shells). We love the details like LED lighting and water features that make the whole experience feel a bit fancy.

Industry observers note that it’s not just about looks, though. With 51 jets and a lounger seat, this tub delivers a more immersive soak than simpler plug-and-play models. The trade-off is in installation. For this model, you’ll need a 240-volt hookup, but that also means those jets will pack a lot of therapeutic power at the end of a long day.

Industry observers note that if you want a five-person hot tub that doesn’t require rewiring your backyard, the LifeSmart LS500 keeps things simple. It plugs into a standard outlet, sets up rapidly, and still delivers a comfortable soak with 23 adjustable jets and a lounge seat. We wish there were more, but other features (and price) make up for the lack of bubbles.

The full-foam insulation and thermal locking cover do a solid job holding heat, which helps keep operating costs in check, and the built-in ozonator cuts down on chemical maintenance. We also like the simple look of this spa, which feels a little high-end for the price bracket. It’s not the most powerful spa in this size range, and heat-up times can be slow, but for an easy, low-hassle setup, it’s a practical upgrade.

While Bestway’s Toronto was our pick for overall best inflatable hot tub, the foam walls do require some extra setup—the process takes two people several hours to complete. On the other hand, the Hot Springs model fully self-inflates in under five minutes and is truly plug-and-play, making it a great choice for those who are purchasing their first hot tub and are not yet familiar with some of the intricacies involved with setting one up and maintaining it.

Everything you need to set it up is included right in the box, with just a level, dry surface and access to an outlet (without an extension cord) required. Despite the lack of foam inserts, this hot tub is still rated for year-round use with Bestway’s Freeze Shield technology. One caveat: While this tub notes it's for four to six people, it's really most practical for just four.

Industry observers note that the DoCred inflatable hot tub delivers solo relaxation without swallowing up a small patio or using a ton of water. Think of it as an outdoor bathtub, perfect for homes with only showers or those with very limited outdoor space. The oval shape actually makes it easier to fully stretch out compared to some two-to-four-person circular models, and the included side table and mat are a nice touch.

A few drawbacks: Because the heater and bubble jets share the same pump and limited electrical power, activating the bubbles pauses the heating function until the massage cycle ends. That just means you’ll need to make sure the tub is at your desired temp before turning on the jets. This tub also isn’t rated for cold-weather use outdoors, so think of it as a fun addition to your warm-weather outdoor vibe.

There are two main types of hot tubs: plug-and-play models and hardwired spas. When we reached out to Courter, he recommended considering several factors before making a decision about which type of hot tub you should go for.

Sources indicate that “The right choice depends less on preference and more on your setup, budget, and how much installation you’re willing to deal with,” states Courter. “There are many things specific to the hot tub being purchased. Things such as whether it is insulated, and what R-value does that insulation have?” R-value measures how well a hot tub’s insulation resists heat loss. The higher the R-value, the better it holds heat, and the less energy it uses to stay warm.

Recent findings suggest that he notes that some hot tubs run on gas, though for this guide we’ve chosen only electric models. Where you live matters, too. “Ambient temperature will play a big part in operational costs,” he says. “The longer a hot tub runs, the more expensive it is to maintain.”.

Recent findings suggest that plug-and-play hot tubs are the easiest way in. Most run on a standard 110-volt outlet, so setup is straightforward. They require no electrician, no buried lines, and no major prep beyond a flat surface.

It has been revealed that they’re typically made from molded plastic and are widely available online, which helps keep prices down. There are also some inflatable models on the market for less permanent use.

The trade-off, however, is performance. These models often have slower heating and less powerful jets compared with higher-end models. Still, for many homes (and especially rentals), this is the most practical option.

Hardwired spas require more planning. These usually run on 240 volts and need professional installation, but they deliver stronger jets, faster heating, and a more refined overall experience.

It has been revealed that most hardwired tubs have acrylic shells and insulated cabinets, which improves durability and efficiency. They also cost more upfront (and installation adds to that), but they feel closer to a traditional showroom spa experience.

If you’re worried about party-hosting capabilities, be wary. Capacity numbers can be misleading. A “six-person” tub will rarely feel comfortable with six adults. If you have the space, it’s usually worth sizing up.

A four-person model works well for one or two people who want room to stretch out, while six- or seven-person tubs are better for families or hosting. If you’re mainly using it for relaxation or hydrotherapy, a smaller tub is easier to maintain, and often more comfortable day to day.

Take time to think about jet count, but that’s not always a straightforward metric on which to judge a hot tub. What matters just as much is the placement, variety, and adjustability of those jets. Higher-powered pumps will provide stronger flow, as well. A lounger with carefully placed jets is a must if you’re seeking physical relief for aches and pains.

In a recent development, it’s fun to have perks like lights and sound systems, but those matter less than the features that keep a hot tub up and running for years. A good cover in particular makes a significant difference. It helps retain heat, reduce energy use, and keep maintenance manageable.

Sources indicate that but once you’ve chosen the size and key mechanical specs that meet your needs, it’s okay to jazz up the experience a bit with neat extras like waterfalls and lights. Just be mindful of additional maintenance. It’s easier to buy a upcoming portable Bluetooth speaker than it is to repair one integrated into a hot tub.

Courter remarked that the exact operational cost is hard to guesstimate—a lot of factors come into play. “The longer a hot tub runs, the more expensive it is to maintain,” he claims. “In Northern Utah, we can get down to minus 10 degrees Fahrenheit in the wintertime. In that same timeframe, the average temperature in Miami is going to be in the mid-70s. A hot tub in northern Utah is going to need to run much more often to maintain its temperature.”.

Industry observers note that when it comes to chemicals and cost, that also varies depending on the size of the hot tub and how often you use it. General online user reports vary between $40 and $100 a month, but it’s not a number that’s easy to estimate. The initial setup will cost a bit more as you invest in the chemicals and supplies you’ll regularly need.

Recent findings suggest that while hot tubs certainly are not a set-it-and-forget-it luxury, they are easier to maintain than a pool—and upkeep should not be a major deterrent. “Maintenance of a hot tub isn’t too bad if you stay on top of it,” says Courter. “Usually, it takes 10 to 20 minutes once a week to adjust your chemicals and clean your filters.”.

Industry observers note that when it comes to chemical options, whether you choose chlorine, bromine, copper, a salt system, or an ozone generator, they all work just fine—as long as you keep your pH in line. “A pH of 7 on the pH scale is neutral, but the pH of a human eye is 7.5, so I always suggest to my customers that they aim for around 7.5,” claims Courter.

Recent findings suggest that other maintenance will involve keeping an eye on the water level, the condition of the hardware, and any signs of malfunction. Some hot tub repairs are simple and you can even DIY them, but many require calling an expert.

Other than structural considerations if you want it on an elevated deck, the options are virtually endless.

“A factory-built hot tub can go just about anywhere, as long as whatever you are putting it on can hold the weight,” says Courter. “A dry hot tub can weigh around 1,000 pounds, but remember that water weighs 8.34 pounds per gallon.” That means an average-sized spa could weigh nearly two tons.

When it comes to ground placement, a flat and level surface with a good base is fine for most uses. If you do choose to place a plug-and-play spa inside your home, be prepared to consult an expert about ways to mitigate moisture damage.

In a recent development, this is another one of those tricky metrics to guesstimate. We’ve listed the warranty windows for each tub we’ve included, but these spas should last longer than that.

Recent findings suggest that “As with most items, it really depends on the quality of the product you buy,” says Courter. He says not all hot tubs are created equal and that consumer research goes a long way. That being said, spending more doesn’t guarantee a longer life for the hot tub.

“If a customer buys the highest-quality tub on the market and doesn't take care of it, it will fail swiftly,” says Courter. “I have seen many hot tubs fail in just a couple of years if not maintained the way they should. In contrast, my wife and I still use a Watkins Hot Springs that is over 25 years old. Moral of the story: Buy the best quality that you can and take care of it.”.

#42796. The Sky This Week from November 20 to 27: Uranus at opposition

The Sky This Week from November 20 to 27: Uranus at opposition

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2072 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that friday, November 20The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M.
  • According to recent reports, in the northeast, Auriga the Charioteer is above the horizon by 7 P.M.
  • Capella’s name essentially means “She-Goat,” according to the late stellar expert Jim Kaler.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that friday, November 20The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST, then passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. They remain visible all evening, forming a triangle in southern Pisces and northern Cetus. The Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, but Neptune will be invisible without binoculars or a telescope. Check out last week’s column for more details on how to view the celestial trio.

According to recent reports, in the northeast, Auriga the Charioteer is above the horizon by 7 P.M. local time. Its brightest star is Capella, which shines at magnitude 0.1 and sits some 43 light-years away. Just southeast of this star, you’ll find another triangle in the sky tonight. This small shape is an asterism about 2.7° long, known as the Kids. It consists of Epsilon (ε), Zeta (ζ), and Eta (η) Aurigae, which range from 3rd (Epsilon and Eta) to 4th (Zeta) magnitude.

Why are these called the Kids? Capella’s name essentially means “She-Goat,” according to the late stellar expert Jim Kaler. These fainter stars cluster close by the brighter star like goat kids around their mother.

Sources indicate that mercury reaches greatest western elongation (20°) at 7 P.M. EST; it will be visible before dawn tomorrow morning, so keep reading for more details.

Sources indicate that sunrise: 6:51 A.M. Sunset: 4:40 P.M. Moonrise: 2:04 P.M. Moonset: 2:12 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (84%) *Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

According to recent reports, saturday, November 21If you’ve got a viewing site with a clear eastern horizon, this morning offers a great opportunity to spot the solar system’s innermost planet. Look for Mercury about an hour before sunrise, when it reaches 7° high and shines at magnitude –0.5. The planet reached its greatest western elongation from our Sun yesterday evening, and is now 20° west of our star in the sky.

Recent findings suggest that located in Libra, the tiny world sits to the far lower left of bright Venus, higher in the sky. Venus is in the constellation Virgo, standing just north (to the upper left) of the bright star Spica. Another bright star, Arcturus in Boötes, hangs to that pair’s far upper left.

Pull out a telescope to check out the size and phase of each planet. Start with Venus, whose disk spans a hefty 46” — currently larger than Jupiter’s apparent size in our sky. Despite its impressive width, however, the disk of Venus appears as just a sliver, only 19% lit. Slide down to Mercury for comparison, and see that its phase is much larger — 62% — while the planet’s overall apparent width is much smaller, just 7”.

Industry observers note that if you’re able, keep watching Mercury day by day in the morning sky. Its gibbous phase will continue growing, reaching 84% lit by the end of the month.

Industry observers note that sunrise: 6:52 A.M. Sunset: 4:39 P.M. Moonrise: 2:29 P.M. Moonset: 3:22 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (92%).

It has been revealed that sunday, November 22With the Moon not far from Full, its western limb is now coming into view as the Sun rises across the lunar landscape. The large, flat-floored crater Schickard is prominent in the southwest, near the small, circular Mare Humorum. Because the nearly Full Moon is so bright, you may want to use a Moon filter before you turn your telescope toward our satellite tonight for a closer look.

Industry observers note that zoom in on Schickard to discover that its dark floor isn’t perfectly smooth, but pockmarked by smaller craters that came after the initial, larger crater’s formation. Its outer walls are shallow and beaten down, also showing off their age. Look closely at Schickard’s western wall to see how it has slumped, particularly compared to the eastern side of the crater rim. Also compare the texture of the southwestern portion of the crater floor, which appears quite rough, to the rest of the crater, which is smoother. The difference arises because most of the crater was flooded by lava, which didn’t quite reach its southwestern regions.

According to recent reports, stretching about 130 miles (210 kilometers) across, Schickard is roughly 4 billion years old and was formed by a giant impact. Because it sits so near the limb of the Moon, it often looks oblong from our vantage point on Earth — but from above, orbiters have shown it is really quite circular in shape.

In a recent development, sunrise: 6:53 A.M. Sunset: 4:39 P.M. Moonrise: 2:59 P.M. Moonset: 4:34 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (97%).

Recent findings suggest that monday, November 23A few hours after sunset, the house-shaped constellation Cepheus stands on the point of its roof in the northern sky, above the Little Dipper. Cepheus is home to several lovely double stars, including Xi (ξ) Cephei, also known as Kurhah.

Glowing at magnitude 4.3, Kurhah is not one of the stars in the house’s outline, but lies within the boxy base. You can find it about midway between Alderamin (Alpha [α] Cep) and Iota (ι) Cep, the western and eastern points in the house’s box, respectively. Kurhah’s two components are separated by just under 8” — once you find the star in binoculars or your finder scope, any telescope will split them. The pair consists of a brighter magnitude 4.4 primary, which glows white, and a fainter magnitude 6.5 secondary, which appears to many observers as yellow.

If you happen to have a large telescope, you may want to give a nearby deep-sky treasure a try: planetary nebula NGC 7139 sits just 2° west-southwest of Kurhah, but it requires a large scope (8 inches at least) to spot, as this bubble of gas glows at magnitude 13.3. If available, an Oxygen-III filter will help bring it out by dimming the nearby stars.

Sunrise: 6:54 A.M. Sunset: 4:38 P.M. Moonrise: 3:37 P.M. Moonset: 5:52 A.M. Moon Phase: Full.

According to recent reports, tuesday, November 24Full Moon occurs at 9:54 A.M. EST, bringing us our second Super Moon of the year. A Super Moon occurs when the Moon reaches Full phase close to perigee, its closest point to Earth, making our satellite appear larger and brighter than average. The November Full Moon is also called the Beaver Moon.

Recent findings suggest that A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars. This is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope (just note that you may want a Moon filter if available, as our satellite is so significant and bright). The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

Sources indicate that the 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed quickly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. The latter two may be difficult to catch from the Midwest without optical aid, as sunrise is fast approaching. If you are using binoculars or a telescope in this region, make sure to put them away several minutes ahead of sunrise from your location. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

For specific timings from your location, visit the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

It has been revealed that the Moon then passes 5° north of Uranus (also in Taurus) at 2 P.M. EST. Over in the constellation Leo, Mars passes 1.8° north of Regulus at 5 P.M. EST.

Recent findings suggest that sunrise: 6:55 A.M. Sunset: 4:38 P.M. Moonrise: 4:24 P.M. Moonset: 7:10 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (99%).

Wednesday, November 25The Moon reaches perigee, the closest point to Earth in its orbit, at 4:01 P.M. EST. At that time, our satellite will stand 223,288 miles (359,347 km) away.

According to recent reports, the distant ice giant Uranus reaches opposition tonight at 6 P.M. EST. Opposition is the best time to view a planet in our sky, and it’s visible roughly from dusk until dawn. Because Uranus is faint — magnitude 5.6 — you’ll want to give it a few hours after sunset to climb away from both light pollution and turbulent air near the horizon. Around 10 P.M. local time, you’ll find Uranus midway between the bright star Aldebaran and the Pleiades star cluster in Taurus the Bull, about 60° above the southeastern horizon. It sits some 1.5° south of 4th-magnitude 37 Tauri.

Although Uranus can be visible to the naked eye under clear, dark conditions, the bright waning Moon is nearby, so pull out binoculars or a telescope to view the far-off planet tonight. Once you land on its location, look for a “flat,” grayish-colored star. Uranus’ disk spans 4”, so you will likely be able to tell it is circular, rather than a pinpoint of light like any background stars.

Sunrise: 6:56 A.M. Sunset: 4:37 P.M. Moonrise: 5:24 P.M. Moonset: 8:26 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (96%).

Recent findings suggest that thursday, November 26Celebrate Thanksgiving with a celestial turkey: The famous Orion Nebula (M42) is also playfully known as the Turkey Nebula because it looks to some like a turkey, particularly in deep astrophotos. But whether you’re a photographer or not, this bright deep-sky treat is easy to enjoy tonight while dinner digests.

Industry observers note that by about 9 P.M. local time, Orion the Hunter has risen above the eastern horizon, his recognizable three-star belt standing in a vertical line. The lowest star in that line is Alnitak (Zeta [ζ] Orionis), and the Orion Nebula lies just 3.7° south-southwest of this star, to its lower right on the sky this evening. You might be able to spot its glow without optical aid, although the bright Moon nearby may make that difficult. Binoculars or any telescope will easily show it.

At 4th magnitude and spanning some 85’ by 60’, the Orion Nebula is a huge and bright star-forming region that sits roughly 1,350 light-years from Earth. In the brightest portion of the nebula lies a small grouping of young stars called the Trapezium Cluster. Take your time with this gorgeous sight, scanning around the region to pick out detail in the nebulosity. And if you are an astrophotographer, consider turning the view into a Thanksgiving memory to share for years to come.

Sunrise: 6:58 A.M. Sunset: 4:37 P.M. Moonrise: 6:35 P.M. Moonset: 9:33 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (91%).

Friday, November 27The Moon-free window for observing Comet 161P/Hartley-IRAS reopens tonight, the same day the comet reaches perihelion, the closest point to the Sun in its 21½-year orbit. It has been a fairly stable 10th to 11th magnitude, and although it has no appreciable tail, the nucleus’ green glow has been notable in recent astrophotos.

You’ll find Hartley-IRAS in the west a few hours after sunset. Around 7 P.M. local time it is still 30° high, well above the turbulent air near the ground that can muddy astronomical views. Tonight the comet is in western Sagitta, about 6.3° north-northeast of 3rd-magnitude Zeta (ζ) Aquilae. Even a small (4-inch) scope will net you a view, but larger apertures will show more detail around the nucleus, allowing you to look for features such as a sharpened southern flank as it flies into the solar headwind.

According to recent reports, while you’re in this region, make sure to sweep just 2.1° northeast of the comet’s location to spot the famous Coathanger asterism in Vulpecula. This 1°-long grouping of stars looks just like its namesake, with the hook on the southern side of the hanger’s arms.

Recent findings suggest that sunrise: 6:59 A.M. Sunset: 4:36 P.M. Moonrise: 7:53 P.M. Moonset: 10:26 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (82%).

The Book Lover’s Gift Guide

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (909 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Science News staff devoured books of all kinds this year, on topics ranging from ecology and evolution to the human brain and mathematics.
  • Major thinkers will love Huge Numbers, a fascinating look into the study of large numbers.
  • Staff writer Erin Garcia de Jesús’ favorite book of 2026, The Creatures’ Guide to Caring, will strike a chord with newly introduced parents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Anna Mattson and Science News Staff.

Science News staff devoured books of all kinds this year, on topics ranging from ecology and evolution to the human brain and mathematics. We covered it all — even a cookbook! These 10 titles rose to the top of our 2026 reading list and could make great gifts for the book lovers in your life. —  Anna Mattson, Assistant Editor.

Major thinkers will love Huge Numbers, a fascinating look into the study of large numbers. “When I think of big numbers, I usually think of a 1 with a lot of zeroes tacked on the end. But the reality is much more complex than I ever imagined,” claims senior physics writer Emily Conover. The book, among Conover’s favorites of the year, “provided me with a newly introduced appreciation of our number system and the creative ways mathematicians have expanded it to express ever-larger numbers,” she says. “Plus, contemplating unfathomably large figures makes my own concerns seem insignificant.”.

Staff writer Erin Garcia de Jesús’ favorite book of 2026, The Creatures’ Guide to Caring, will strike a chord with newly introduced parents. “Between sleepless nights and poopy diapers, there’s not much to laugh about in the early days of parenting. But I found plenty of humor (and plenty to be grossed out about) in The Creatures’ Guide to Caring,” Garcia de Jesús says. “It’s the perfect book to make anyone, parent or otherwise, feel better that we’re not the only animals struggling with our offspring.”.

Merritt R. TuretskyW.W. Norton & Organization | $29.99.

Adventure seekers will lose themselves in the mesmerizing ecosystems at the heart of Bogland, biomedical sciences writer Aimee Cunningham’s favorite book of the year. Ecologist Merritt R. Turetsky immerses readers in these waterlogged landscapes that are often overlooked and underestimated. “I am firmly on team boglands after reading about the beauty and wonder of these ecosystems,” Cunningham indicates.

Saul Justin NewmanThe MIT Press | $29.95.

In a recent development, senior writer Meghan Rosen’s favorite book of 2026 is perfect for anyone interested in — or wary of — health and wellness culture. Morbid exposes the lack of science behind a lot of antiaging advice, such as eating like centenarians do and taking “anti­aging” supplements. “Turns out, a lot of it is just plain bunk,” Rosen claims. “Skeptical readers will enjoy Newman’s takedowns, which go down smoothly with a healthy dose of humor.”.

Susana CarmonaThe MIT Press | $27.95.

Senior neuroscience writer Laura Sanders’ pick for 2026 is a must-read for any expecting mother, latest mother or person looking to learn about how pregnancy and motherhood impact the body. “A Mother’s Brain reads like a scientific love letter to moms, who all too often get overlooked,” she claims. Author and neuroscientist Susana Carmona “covers the nascent field of matrescence in lively, vivid chapters. And along the way, she convincingly argues that the maternal brain is compelling, wondrous and still mysterious,” Sanders says.

Aaron MahnkeRunning Press | $30.00.

Industry observers note that those who listen to true crime podcasts or wish spooky season lasted all year long will enjoy Exhumed, an exploration of the lore and medical practices leading up to the 19th century Fresh England vampire panic. “Thanks to Mahnke’s gripping prose, I felt like I was in the middle of the action. It was hard to lay the book down,” assistant editor Anna Mattson wrote in her online review. Mattson notes that Exhumed, her favorite read of 2026, is littered with bizarre facts that would be perfect for invigorating dull conversations.

Sources indicate that for the anthropologist in your life, try The Story of Stories — a deep dive into how technological upheavals have shaped storytelling throughout history. The author provides what Sanders describes as scattershot history lessons in her online review: “Ashton has a knack for pulling out memorable bits from historical records, scientific studies and other sources for readers.”.

Alexis Nikole NelsonSimon & Schuster | $35.00.

Conover couldn’t pick just one favorite. For people who enjoy getting creative in the kitchen, she recommends Happy Snacking, Don’t Die! “This cookbook provides such a joyful how-to on foraging and eating wild plants,” Conover claims. “It helped me see my plant neighbors in a whole upcoming light. And I got to make some tasty treats to share with my family as well.”.

In a recent development, riley BlackSt. Martin’s Press | $29.00.

Recent findings suggest that tyrant Lizard Queen is the only work of fiction on our list. But it’s rooted in real science, and stars a Tyrannosaurus rex. Author Riley Black “offers an empathetic look at a real-life creature that experienced hunger and pain, much like the animals that surround us today,” states Science News Explores assistant editor Aaron Tremper, who chose the book as his favorite of 2026. “Black’s penchant for story makes for a thrilling read that fans of Jurassic Park and King Kong can get behind.”.

Joshua D. MezrichThe MIT Press | $29.95.

And for those interested in bioethics, we suggest picking up Every Living Creature. Author and physician Joshua D. Mezrich offers a comprehensive look at the field of xenotransplantation, through the stories of courageous doctors and patients who helped make it possible. “At times, the story can feel like a whirlwind, whisking readers across decades and from lab to lab and surgery to surgery,” Rosen wrote in her online review. “But at its core, Every Living Creature is a book about hope.”.
